subsubtopic: PROCEDURE ON MOTION TO ESTABLISH JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as announced last week the business for both today and tomorrow will be a debate on the motion to establish a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the constitution, which stands in the Prime Minister's name which is now under government notices of motions and which it is assumed will be transferred in due course to government orders today. There have been discussions among the parties as to the procedure for handling this matter and I think there might be found to be general agreement for a special order to deal with this debate.
The first characteristic of it would be that the ordinary time limits provided under Standing Order 31 would be suspended, that an initial spokesman for each of the parties would be entitled to speak for 40 minutes and that thereafter speakers would be entitled to speak for 20 minutes. Second, the debate would be a two-day debate and all questions necessary to a decision on the motion would be put immediately before the ordinary time for adjournment on the second day.
There has also been a suggestion, and unfortunately I have not had full opportunity to consult on this point, that on each of the two days private members' hour might be suspended in order to allow maximum opportunity for participation. I wonder if that might be agreeable and if that could be a special order of the House?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, January 19, the hon. member for Hamilton West directed a question to me and to the Prime Minister regarding allegations of racial discrimination in Canada. I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity of making a statement on this important matter and of expressing what I hope is the view of all hon. members of the House.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Since the incident which occurred at the Sir George Williams University computer centre in February, 1969, various statements have been made, both in Canada and in the Caribbean, by some of those accused of offences in connection with that incident and by other persons with an interest in the matter, alleging that Canada has a racist society and pursues racialist policies. As hon. members are aware, such statements are without foundation. The fact that the Canadian government does not engage in, and will not tolerate in any department or agency for which it is responsible, policies which involve discrimination on grounds of race, creed, colour or ethnic origin is well known. Furthermore, as an adherent to the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights, and a signatory of the international convention on the elimination of all forms of racial discrimination, Canada has affirmed its opposition to such discrimination. The government reiterates its fullest support of these principles and objectives.
2790

January 26, 1970
Racial Discrimination
Since the events of February, 1969, I have met on several occasions with a number of people interested in the Sir George Williams University incident. At one such meeting with a group of students and professors, I gave them the government's assurance that the events at Sir George would in no way affect Canadian government policy with regard to the admission of Caribbean students or the functioning of Canadian educational assistance programs. I have also met twice with diplomatic representatives of the Commonwealth countries of the Caribbean, when I assured them that our immigration regulations and policies would not be altered as a result of these events. I also expressly made the point that the incident at Sir George Williams University should not be allowed to damage relations between Canada and their countries.
Racial discrimination is a cancerous growth which gnaws away the humanity of society and is an example of what Robert Burns called "man's inhumanity to man". Canada is not free from racial prejudice. In this, as in all countries, there are people who practise racial discrimination. Racial discrimination arises from ignorance and fear. It cannot be eradicated by Acts of Parliament or regulations, although these can and do restrain its more extreme manifestations.
The Canadian government is opposed to racism in any form and is working to create the conditions in which our society will be free of it. The government cannot carry out this task alone. It calls for the best efforts of all Canadians of good will. Parents and teachers, who form the attitudes of the young, bear a special responsibility.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak not only for members on this side of the House but all hon. members who are concerned about the problem of discrimination because of race, creed or colour when I say I am pleased that the government has stood up to be counted throughout the world for the benefit of those who have the attitude that our eyes continue to be closed to the ultimate results. This has now been discounted. Unquestionably there are many in our great country who continue to practice acceptance of a man on the basis of race, creed or colour. This must stop.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES
speechtext:
We have seen the results of such an attitude in other countries which I need not mention. Those who continue to

adhere to this philosophy must realize the harm that can come to this country. We must maintain our good relations with the West Indies because there is mutual benefit from such a relationship.
I am pleased to see that the House generally has accepted the spirit of my question. I am also pleased that Canada has stood up to be counted as a country that welcomes all people, regardless of race, creed or colour, who want to come to this country in freedom and take part productively by becoming an actual and viable force in the mainstream of Canadian life.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ALLEGED BY CERTAIN STUDENTS FROM WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We have always supported the international conventions of the United Nations and of the International Labour Organization. Canada itself has fair employment practices legislation and the Bill of Rights on its statute books, and we support the principles enunciated in the minister's statement.
We welcome particularly the statement that despite what happened at Sir George Williams University the government has no intention of altering its policy under which Caribbean students have been admitted in large numbers to study in Canada.
Without expressing any view on the trials now in progress, or on some of the things which happened at Sir George Williams- indeed, it would be improper for me to comment on the trials at this point-I express the hope that when the trials have been completed and the students have paid the penalty, if any, meted out by the courts, the government of Canada, through the Department of Manpower and Immigration, will' avoid taking a very legalistic approach to this matter. I trust it will not arrange for the automatic deportation of these people as it has a right to do when crimes have been committed and convictions obtained.
There is one further point I should like to make, though it does not relate directly to the responsibility of the federal government. It seems to us that the decision of the university to bar from registration this year the students who have been charged, before they have been convicted or given an opportunity to defend themselves and explain what happened, is wrong. To a certain extent at least they have, in fact, been tried and found guilty by the university, and for this reason we believe the course taken is wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank sincerely the Secretary of State for External Affairs, on behalf of my colleagues, for the statement he has just made in respect of racism.
I appreciated the statement made by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). May I say that I am proud of his participation in the business of the House, because, once more, I repeat, once more this proves that any person, regardless of his race or his color, can take an efficient part, not only in the business of the State, but also in the administration and the operation of a State.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the real issue is not simply a matter of race, colour or creed, but rather a problem of individuals. Since Canada throws her doors open to all sorts of individuals, the presence of a certain foreigner in Canada at this time is worrying a lot of people, especially some ministers of the province of Quebec. I rather think it is in that field that Canada should enforce strict supervision in order to prevent some trouble makers from infiltrating into our country.

speechtext:
1. The Canadian Government Travel Bureau uses a computer system to type letters in answer to requests for travel information about Canada. Trained personnel first review all such requests, to determine whether they may be answered through the computer system, utilizing prepared letters or a selection of prepared paragraphs stored in the computer memory bank, or whether the enquiries require individually dictated replies. It is also possible that the counsellor's instructions to the computer could be incorrectly transcribed or acted on in the preparation of the punchcard which activates the computer printer.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has not made any statement concerning his talks with the Right Hon. speakeroldname: Righi Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we did discuss many subjects, including the last one mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition. We talked about Nigeria, we talked about east-west relations, we talked about disarmament, and we talked about the SALT talks. We also went into the question of Britain's entry into the Common Market, and the ministers present, particularly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, pressed several questions upon Prime Minister Wilson concerning the consequences for Canada of Britain's negotiations to enter the Common Market.

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Did the government of Canada take any specific position with regard to Canadian trade in the event that Britain should enter the European Common Market? In other words, did the government of Canada present a specific proposition to the government of Great Britain with regard to this matter?

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: Specific, Mr. Speaker, only to the extent that we pressed on the Prime Minister the importance of keeping Canada informed about the negotiations as they proceed and as they affect Canada. It was difficult to be more specific than that on specific items for the simple reason that the Prime Minister himself avowed that he did not know how the discussions would proceed. Therefore until the British government itself has had further contacts with the members of the EEC, and until it has formulated its position and stated it, it is impossible for Canada to enter upon specifics.

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, did the Prime Minister not outline the specific and important areas of Canadian trade which would be very adversely affected if the Commonwealth preference was lost in the event that Britain entered the common market? Did the Prime Minister not ask for and receive assurances regarding Canadian trading arrangements with Great Britain in order that these important trading arrangements can be maintained and protected?

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we pressed upon the government of the United Kingdom and the Prime Minister the importance of the specific aspects of trade with Canada. I repeat, we could not draw any conclusions from the Prime Minister as to these points because, as he emphasized, he himself had not actually begun negotiations yet. So far as Canadian representations are concerned, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself did emphasize aspects of Britain's entry which would be very important to us.

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Prime Minister intend to send the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to Great Britain very soon to ask for these specific assurances he was not able to receive from the British Prime Minister?

subtopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-REPRESENTATIONS TO PRIME MINISTER WILSON
speechtext: We doubt whether the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce could get from the rest of the British government assurances that the Prime Minister himself asked us to wait a while before receiving.

He said:

Mr. Speaker, it is a question of considering the motion standing in my name on the order paper, but I think that hon. members will want to take this opportunity to discuss the whole process of constitutional review. Indeed, at the time of the last public federal-provincial conferences on the constitution, the House deemed it appropriate to discuss the process of constitutional review, and following the December conference, leaders of all parties agreed to initiate this debate on the constitution.

We are faced, in a sense, with a paradox when we face this motion. The presence of this motion on the order paper is indicative of the interest of all parties in debating the process of constitutional review in this chamber. Indeed, parties of the opposition have pressed the government for many months, and even over a period of two sessions, to set up this committee. I believe that this reflects on the part of hon. members a very great desire of participating in the constitutional debate taking place in this country. But I spoke of a paradox, because at the same time there is a feeling in certain provincial quarters, and even in the country at large as expressed by members of provincial legislatures and, indeed, perhaps by some members of this House, that there is basically nothing wrong with the present constitution, nothing at least that, would put it very high in priority on the order for action.
There is a feeling indeed in some quarters that this government is a little bit hung up on constitutional matters, that we are giving them too great a priority, that we are spending too much time on the constitution and too little on other things, and that the debate is taking too long. We have even heard in some quarters, and I am merely repeating that in this operation we have in mind only Quebec; that the rest of the country is not very interested in the process of constitutional review. I say this is a paradox, Mr. Speaker, because if we examine the origins of the constitutional debate we will see that it really began at the instigation of the provinces, indeed, of all the provinces. It would be fair to say that they started the process of constitutional debate. They are the ones who-embarked the country on this long and important process. I say this as much to their credit as to their debit because I believe that.

the process of constitutional review is an important process.
It is necessary, however, in order to explain this paradox, to remind ourselves once again that it began at the November 1967 conference, convened by the Prime Minister of Ontario, Mr. Robarts, and which was attended by the premiers of all provinces, barring that of British Columbia which was represented by its attorney general. The provinces at that time pressed the federal government to participate and I think members of opposition parties will recall that they, too, were pressing the government to attend the Confederation for Tomorrow Conference in Toronto. They chided us and urged us to get into the constitutional debate.
Notwithstanding that that was the position of the opposition, the federal government took the contrary view. Not only did we not participate in the 1967 conference, hut in the years prior to that we had taken the very clear position that the constitution was not the most urgent thing to be dealt with, that there were many problems facing Canadians which could be dealt with under the British North America Act. Although we were not prepared to discuss the subject, we urged the provinces and the public at large to regard these exercises with a certain amount of deliberation.
I think the change in attitude on the part of governments is easy to explain, Mr. Speaker. The provinces realized in 1967 that new power relationships were being developed between the federal government and the provinces. It is perhaps natural that they wanted to insert these power relationships into a constitution which would be redefined. Hon. members will recall that around that period the provincial responsibilities in financial terms were increasing at a very fast speed compared to those of the federal government.
Statistics show that between 1954 and 1964 federal expenditures increased 56 per cent. In that same period provincial expenditures, including municipal expenditures, increased 204 per cent. This is evidence of these new relationships that were developing, Mr. Speaker. It is precisely because of that that the federal government was preaching against haste in upsetting the constitutional relationships between the federal government and the provinces until a fair amount of preparatory work had been accomplished.
We realized that once a questioning of the consensus on which the country was built,

began, and once it was agreed upon by Canadians to reopen the fundamental law from which all authority and power flowed in this country, it would be impossible to close that issue until we had dealt with it thoroughly. This was the position taken by the government under the leadership of hon. L. B. Pearson. It certainly was the position of many members on this side of the House.
/ I, personally, went on record as saying that rof all the urgent problems facing Canada, in my view the constitution had lowest priority. In September, 1967, a couple of months before the Confederation for Tomorrow Conference, I was speaking to the Canadian Bar Association in Quebec city. I told them we should be very careful before opening the basis for all law, order and authority within the country, that we should do our homework first. I emphasized the need for preparation in order that changes in the basic and fundamental law would be orderly and progressive and not arrived at piecemeal, bit by bit. That is why I proposed on that same occasion, with the approval of the government of that day, that we begin with a discussion of a fundamental Bill of Rights in order to ascertain the values which united Canadians before going on to issues which might divide them.
This is the paradox that has to be explained, Mr. Speaker. We should not forget the urging on the part of the provinces and, I repeat, of the opposition, for the government to get on with writing a new constitution for Canada. We remember all the cliches of those days; that the constitution was 100 years old that it did not read well; that we should have a more inspiring document for our centennial, and that the previous government was lax in its desire to get on with this review. Nevertheless-and this is the paradox, Mr. Speaker-in addition to these pressures, we began to hear more and more from the provinces and other quarters that this whole constitutional thing was a hang-up of the federal government; that the present government was too concerned with these matters and should be getting on with other things. How does one explain this paradox?

Canadian Constitution
and that the solutions cannot wait until a new constitution is drafted.
This process of increasing provincial powers was foreseeable. We live in a civilization, in an industrial society, whose industrialization rate tends to increase. I feel it is true to say that Canada is perhaps one of the countries with the fastest industrialization and urbanization rate in the world. And I think that urban growth has caused a great number of problems, particularly at the municipal level. We have witnessed, for example, problems relating to welfare, slum clearance, air and water pollution in the cities, housing, urban transportation, fire and police services, water supply, telephone and communication systems, even recreational activities which have brought cities to provide more parks, more recreational centres and more libraries. These problems all emerged at the municipal level and therefore were also of provincial jurisdiction. I believe that after several years of debate on constitutional matters some provinces and municipalities realize that they really have much left to do and that all these problems must find a solution before the constitution is to be revamped. I think this is the reason why the provinces and municipalities very frequently suggest that the constitution is really of relative importance and that the federal government should not spend too much time considering it.
On the other hand, we cannot, at the federal level, take that position, because we are, by the very nature of federalism, elected to deal with national unity. Indeed, we are commissioned to consider the problems that might lead to the disruption of Canada as a whole.
It might be advisable at this time to quote a letter that Sir John A. Macdonald wrote in 1886 to the Lieutenant-Governor of Nova Scotia. This will help explain that at that time as it is today, it was normal for federal members of Parliament to concern themselves with constitutional matters more than would be the case for members of the Legislative Assemblies. Here is the letter:
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

Should your ministers found their advice for an early dissolution on the ground that they desire an immediate expression of the will of the people as to their remaining in the confederation, you will, I have no doubt, feel it your duty as a Dominion Officer to decline to allow that subject to enter into consideration at all. The representatives of Nova Scotia as to all questions respecting the relations between the Dominion and the Province sit in the Dominion Parliament and are the constitutional exponents of the wishes of the people with regard to 21611-39
such relations. The Provincial members have their powers restricted to the subjects mentioned in the British North America Act and can go no further.

The quotation is to be found at page 379 of Pope's collection of the correspondence of Sir John A. Macdonald.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that quotation explains that at that time as well as today, it was natural for the federal members to have a greater interest in constitutional issues because they have as it were the prime responsibility to ensure that this country is going ahead, all the while maintaining unity in every part.
As to national unity, Mr. Speaker, it is important to mention that it is not only a problem which affects the province of Quebec, and which deals mainly with language issues. Indeed linguistic differences between the French-speaking and the English-speaking communities raise a problem insofar as national unity is concerned. The government of the right hon. Lester B. Pearson as well as ours have always squarely tackled the study of this problem. The solutions we have recommended in the field of bilingualism and the legislation of this session are recognized, I believe, as a major contribution towards maintaining national unity.
Admittedly, national unity also involves certain economic aspects: disparities between regions and between the various classes of society can contribute to destroy national unity just as much as linguistic issues can. This is why our government has taken important initiatives concerning regional economic expansion and its powers to spend, not only as regards the overall power to spend through which we transfer certain financial resources to provincial governments by way of equalization payments or otherwise, but also as regards the power to pay certain allowances directly to less fortunate people in order that the more affluent Canadians be more adequately taxed, which will contribute to maintaining a regular income for Canadians.
Another aspect of national unity has to do with the very geography of the country and the scattering of the population; today, as in the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, we have to tackle straight off the problem of communications. At that time, it had to do mostly with the railways, and then the telegraph. But we realize that today the problem of communications covers a much wider field. In fact, not only people, but messages and information have to be conveyed to their destina-

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
tion. It will be with that in mind that this session will have reviewed the policy of the government in this connection.
Finally, national unity is embodied in the federal-provincial relations I dealt with earlier and which brought this government to take on still more energetically constitutional matters. The point is not to believe that the federal-provincial meetings on the constitution alone tackle the problems of national unity. In fact, the federal government took it upon itself to call a conference next February-that is in three weeks-not on constitutional problems but on federal-provincial relations in non-constitutional fields.
Surely, these are as many facets of the more general problem of national unity. While considering them, we can see that if a country is to survive, it should solve the constantly recurring problem of national unity.

In other words, the unity of a country can only be built up on the basis of a consensus of the people, on the desire of the people to live together within the boundaries of the same country. I think modern history has shown us that there is really no other basis for national unity than this. It is impossible to hold that countries are the product of boundaries which are given by nature and which cannot be moved, and that the people living within those boundaries must forever form a country because those boundaries were destined to the people by the laws of nature and of God. We have only to look at our own boundaries, at the 49th parallel or the Alaskan panhandle, to realise that there is nothing written on the surface of the globe which says that this country was obliged to have these boundaries and that the people living within them were bound to form one nation.
I think it is true, also, to say that speaking the same language is not in itself the foundation of one nation. We know there are nations separated by artificial borders whose inhabitants speak the same language and, conversely, we know there are certain nations within whose boundaries two, three and even four languages are spoken.
It is neither geographical boundaries, nor language, nor, indeed, history which determine the existence of a nation. We are aware that nations are not eternal and that history has changed them all over the centuries. We are, therefore, forced to the conclusion that the only basis for a nation is a consensus, a willingness of people to live together. People

choose to form a nation. There is a nation if the people want a nation to exist. In this sense, the French philosopher Renan can describe a nation as "un plebiscite du peuple de tous les jours"-a plebiscite of the people every day, not in a literal sense but in a literary sense. The people have to be willing to recognize that the nation exists in order that it might continue to exist. This means, in reality, that all major groups, all important participants in a nation, have to feel that they are better within the nation than outside it. So long as we cannot ensure the continuation of this consensus, so long as the institutions of a country and, singularly, the constitution of the country, does not correspond to a desire of the people to stay within a nation, its basis is very frail indeed. It is this principle which guided federal action and, indeed, federal strategy in its whole approach to the constitutional question.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
It was our belief that the nation could only be based on such a consensus that guided us in the process of constitutional review. First, we took as a principle that there was a great deal of preparation needed before the constitutional review should be embarked upon. Indeed, as early as 1966 the federal government was setting up a special section and engaging the services of specialists in order to get on with the preparations for a constitutional review.
The second principle was that the review should not begin until there was both a recognition, and a desire on the part of enough Canadians that the review should not only begin but that the whole area of federal-provincial relations should be re-examined. This, too, explains in part the fact that the federal government made haste slowly in embarking upon the process of review. In our view it would have been a mistake to open the constitution for debate if there were not a widely shared desire on the part of the Canadian people, and of all parties in this Parliament, to embark upon such a review.
Third, it was important that the review only proceed within a country which was fairly stable, and by that I mean at a time when the federal government and the provincial governments were both strong. As far as we were concerned at the federal level, we always made it a condition that the whole of the constitution could be re-examined but that two basic principles had to be maintained.
January 26, 1970

The first was that Canada would continue as one federal country. By this we meant that the federal form of government should be preserved. The second principle was that we did not want to see the development of any constitution which would create forms of special arrangements whereby the members of Parliament from one part of the country would have, at the federal level, less power than the members of Parliament from another part of the country. This did not mean that the federal government could not in the future, as it had in the past, embark upon certain specific special arrangements with one province or another.
But any move towards the so-called special status, Mr. Speaker, a move which would have ended with the setting up of a federal form of government wherein at least one province had much stronger powers or jurisdiction than the other provinces, would inevitably have resulted in a situation where the federal members of Parliament from that province could not speak in the federal government with a voice equal to that of members from other provinces. Inevitably, that would have led to a downgrading of the federal presence from that province. Thereafter the people of that province would have been less interested in their representatives in the federal government, and in its ways and procedures, because their representatives would have less power and less significance than members from other provinces.
I repeat that that is why we always stated as a precondition that the debate on the constitution only be opened at a time when the federal government was sufficiently strong to be able to assert what was needed in order to maintain essential federal powers. But apart from these two principles-that of the maintenance of one federal country, and the other that the central essential powers be maintained-we agreed that all aspects of the constitution should be considered. Indeed, it is important that Canadians realize that we are discussing all of the aspects which are of immediate concern to them, questions which have to do with the responsibility for the cities, for pollution, for poverty, for education, and for Indians. These precise questions are part of the constitutional review upon which we have now embarked. There has always been a willingness, indeed a desire, on the part of the federal government to get into these discussions but this was contained until we had been assured that the new constitution would emanate from a stability and a 21611-395
Canadian Constitution
consensus freely arrived at rather than from violence and revolution.
The fourth principle, Mr. Speaker, is the importance of looking at all aspects of the constitution, but having respect to the two principles I just mentioned.
The fifth is the insistence on the part of the federal government-and I repeat that this is part of our approach, and no doubt one on which the opposition parties will wish to comment-that the debate begin on the values that deal with people and with subjects which unite people rather than divide them. It is this principle that explains why our agenda for the constitution began with a discussion of a fundamental Bill of Rights to be written into the constitution. We felt this was a proper vehicle for all Canadians to discuss the questions of value which unite them.
From there, the next step was to discuss the institutions of government themselves- the authorities and the legal entities set up under the constitution to look after people to preserve their rights, and to defend their rights under the law. This led us to consider the second broad aspect of the constitution.
Only following consideration of these two aspects did the provinces and the federal government feel it wise to place on the agenda the specific issue of the division of powers. We felt, and I believe it was also the feeling of the provinces, that rather than start with a debate of the division of powers between federal and provincial authorities it was important to debate first those values which united Canadians. Fundamentally we believed that Canadians were interested in being well served by all their governments, whether federal or provincial, and that only secondarily were they interested in quarrels regarding authority and influence between these levels of government.
The sixth principle is one of controlled development of the constitution, and I suppose this is a way of explaining why the whole process takes time, Mr. Speaker. There are certain circumstances where a constitution must be written fairly quickly. After a revolution, when anarchy exists, when society has no authority by which to govern itself, it is necessary to get on rather quickly with the constitution, that is to say, with the definition of the power relationships among the various authorities within the country. But we wanted to do it not after a revolution, and' indeed not after the founding of a new country. We wanted to take a country which

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
existed and which had desired to take another look at itself, a second century look at itself, and to re-examine the consensus upon which it existed. We were trying to devise a new constitution for a nation in a period of peace, without upsetting the consensus, without giving cause for violence, or for violent upsurges within the country. This, inevitably, takes a long time to complete.
If the consensus is to be continued, it is certain that all the aspects of the constitution can only be discussed and examined within a process of development which is controlled, which is not haphazard but which is well planned. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the adjustments to the new power relations, if there are to be any in Canada's new constitution, have to be gradual. If the adjustments were to be rapid, it would mean the upset of old power relationships, of institutions and of views, and this is the way of revolutions. Obviously the transfer of any influence, power or authority has to be gradual or otherwise it will not have the consent of the people who believe in the democratic way.
The seventh principle is that, while this long process was continuing, one fundamental principle had to be observed and respected: that was that during the whole process of constitutional review the constitution had to be obeyed.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
If the provinces or the federal government had found themselves authorized to say that, the constitution was up for a new deal, that we were rewriting the fundamental law of Canada, that in the meantime the federal or provincial governments could usurp whatever powers they wanted because this was the way they saw the new constitution in the future, then obviously we would have had chaos. It is for this reason that the policy of the federal government was to insure, as far as it was concerned, total respect of the constitution during the process of constitutional review. We have repeated often enough that the only basis for liberty, freedom and order in our country is the constitution, and that if the constitution is not obeyed by provincial and federal governments there is no reason why citizens should have to obey federal and provincial statutes and laws. That is why, though some quarters have indicated impatience with the federal government's position, that we have always said that until the constitution is changed, and until we agree on a new constitution, this government intends to obey the present constitution.

This leads me to the eighth principle, Mr. Speaker, and this is the last one I want to mention. It is obvious that, during this long process of constitutional review, other priorities must be met. It is important that the people of Canada realize that as far as the government is concerned no program has been delayed because of the constitutional review. I am not saying that there are not some things that we, as the government, have not done because of the constitution. On the contrary, because of the constitution we have not done certain things which we felt were not within our jurisdiction, but we have not delayed any programs on the pretense that the constitution was being debated and we were not sure that we should proceed with them. There are many examples which I could give but which I must shorten. Whether programs concerned minority rights, pollution, Indians or, indeed, many others, we have always taken the position that the federal government would and should discharge its responsibility under the present constitution and would continue to do so until the constitution was changed.
Nor has the process of review precluded federal-provincial meetings on other subjects. This is why the federal government took the initiative of inviting the provinces to the forthcoming February conference where we will be discussing non-constitutional matters.
I reach the end of my intervention at this stage, Mr. Speaker. We are to vote on a motion to set up a parliamentary committee. Let me make three brief points on that motion.
We believe it is the role of the parliamentary committee to review and judge the actions of this government and the position it has taken on the constitution. I think this is a welcome development and it is all the more imperative because of the need for consensus that I was discussing earlier. It will be important for all parties in this Parliament, and indeed, for all people in Canada to review and to judge the actions of this government in the constitutional review.
Legitimacy of a constitution cannot be founded, and will not be founded on force in this country. It can only be founded on consent, and it is this consent that we think can only be the result of a widespread debate on the positions which have been developed by the federal and provincial governments. The parliamentary committee will provide a forum where the Canadian public can learn about and discuss federal proposals. As the
January 26, 1970

Canadian Constitution
terms of reference appear on the order paper, it is apparent that we are encouraging the committee to hold hearings across the country and to become a fundamental part of this process of education of Canadians. I mean by this education, not in the sense of proposing particular principles for government, but education in the sense that people will be invited to evolve for themselves their notions of the principles and consensus on which they want this country to be based.
We know that certain provinces have set up parliamentary committees of their own to examine the proposals put forward by provincial governments. We feel it is quite proper for the federal parliament to have that kind of a parliamentary committee and that kind of a forum. From what I have said, I think it follows that no one expects early results. The committee's work will, I presume, take as long as the review process itself. It is impossible that the committee will be expected, even at this session, or even within the next, to bring in a final report. I take it that the committee, and this is authorized in its terms of reference, will prefer to make periodic reports on specific aspects of the constitution that it has been examining.

Those are the few points I was anxious to make on this subject. I believe that the committee's terms of reference result from the very matters agreed upon between federal and provincial representatives for the process of reviewing the constitution. Should this recommendation be adopted by the House, as I hope it will, the committee will definitely have to assume heavy responsibilities not only toward the House, but also toward the whole country.
And all Canadians, as well as ourselves members of Parliament, will have to exercise great courage, patience, far-sightedness and dedication. We are certainly at a crucial point in the constitutional development of the country, and the eyes of the nation are upon us.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the Prime Minister would permit a question?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we just listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) discussing the problems of the constitution very earnestly apd very quietly. I do not know that I will be able to be quite as quiet as that all the time, but I want to assure the Prime Minister and members of the House that I have never believed in injecting any partisan controversy into a discussion of the constitution. On the other hand, if we are to make progress I think we have to talk to each other quite frankly on occasions such as this.
I enter this debate with quite a strong feeling that this is an occasion of some considerable historic significance. I do not know how many times in recent years or in the past the House has engaged in a full and wide-ranging debate on the constitution. Be that as it may,
I think we are holding this debate at a time when the constitutional discussions initiated by the Government of Canada, through a series of federal-provincial conferences, have bogged down. It seems to me it is not exaggerating at all to say that the successful development of constitutional discussion in this country will depend in a very real way upon the workings of the committee of the House we are about to establish.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Federal-provincial meetings have demonstrated practically no progress. If progress is to be made, it must be made by or at least with the assistance of this committee. I believe we have gone much too far in the direction of turning our constitutional discussions into something so complicated, and perhaps so colourless and lacking in immediate relevance to our people, that even the most important constitutional questions excite very little or no public interest except when they stir some emotions. Of course, when emotions are stirred this does not make it any easier to reach a new consensus. During the past number of years there have been many feder-

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
al-provincial conferences dealing with attempts, some of them successful, to make fundamental changes in the structures and ways by which we govern ourselves. But these federal-provincial conferences have been carried out by heads of government, both provincial and federal, or by persons delegated by the heads of these governments.
Never have Canadians as a whole or as groups been involved in this process; nor have the representatives the people of Canada have elected, either in Parliament, the legislatures or in the local councils, been involved in any meaningful way. So, I hope this committee will give a voice to the views and the actions of the Canadian people. I hope the committee itself will provide opportunities to Canadians everywhere to make their views heard and have them considered and publicized rather than filed away and forgotten.
Today marks the beginning of a change in our approach to constitutional reform in this country. The Prime Minister almost suggested that we entered this process, if not by accident, at least without fully intending to do so. Certainly, the constitution is too important to be left to lawyers, prime ministers and provincial premiers. The change I suppose is not very startling in terms of the experience in other countries. It simply lacks the involvement of the Canadian people to a considerable degree in the constitution and rephasing of our constitutional procedures.
Why should the constitution be significant to the average Canadian? After all, he probably cannot tell one very much about it. So, why not leave it to the constitutional lawyers, the premiers, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) who sometimes professes to know what is best for us. Political authority in a modern state must include more than providing the possibility of using our collective strength to clean up our environment or improve our standard of living or health, important as these matters are. Surely, the political process is the means by which we make the hardest choices we have to make collectively. Quite simply political authority is a life and death affair and our constitutional process is the one workable way we in this country have developed to make sure this life and death authority is organized on terms favourable rather than unfavourable to the Canadian people. This is the reason the constitutional proposals made by the government of Canada cannot and should not be decided upon simply on the basis of government.

Our ministers must not alone decide everything about the way in which we are to be ruled. In any event, it is painfully evident to all of us that the present method of approach outlined by the Prime Minister, that of federal-provincial conferences-federal-provincial conference after federal-provincial conference-is not working. Bringing the public into the discussions through a parliamentary committee might just break this log jam. For some years our party has been pressing for the establishment of such a parliamentary committee on revision of the constitution. It has always seemed to us absurd that serious discussion of constitutional revision should be taking place almost everywhere-not primarily everywhere but any place-other than in this House of Commons and in Parliament. This after all, as the Prime Minister has reminded us, is the only institution which is entitled to speak for all Canadians.
Various provincial legislatures have had either parliamentary committees or citizens committees studying and reporting on constitutional matters. There was a Confederation of Tomorrow conference in 1967, a series of federal-provincial conferences beginning in 1968, the Etats Generaux of Quebec and a great many other privately sponsored conferences and studies of constitutional ideas. But the federal Parliament surely has been left out of this process. Last year the Prime Minister refused to co-operate in the establishment of a committee such as this. I regret this, but am delighted he has changed his mind in the meantime. Obviously, we welcome and will support the motion to set up the committee. It is sad indeed that the committee was not set up long ago, but this can be said: The need for the committee obviously is greater now than the need has been in the past. We have always seen this role as being not just one of study and discussion of various constitutional ideas. It has been our thought and hope all along that the parliamentary committee and, through the committee, Parliament itself might be used as a means of reconciliation and a means of arriving at a national consensus.
I was very interested that the Prime Minister took the time he did to develop the thought that the consensus must lie at the very basis of nationhood. I believe this is so. There is not a consensus in this country today with regard to the constitution. I think we must face this. It has been our hope that a parliamentary committee of this sort, made up of elected representatives representing the
January 26, 1970

various parts of the country and the various ways of life in this country, could help the Canadian people achieve a consensus with regard to the constitution. Let us see if the people's elected representatives, consulting each other, consulting other members of the House and listening to and drawing in the people themselves, can begin the task of overcoming the differences and divisions from which obviously the government of Canada and the provincial governments have suffered in the discussions which have taken place at the federal-provincial conferences. I think this can be a useful way to build an understanding about the basic issues which will knit Canadians together and not divide them.
This means the committee must hear groups and individuals from all across the country. The committee evidently has this power. The results of public hearings and consultations with the people sometimes are somewhat painful and a little surprising, but whether this be so or not these public hearings and consultations are necessary to the process of building a real understanding of the problems. There is one important group of elected people who, besides members of the House of Commons, have been almost entirely left out of constitutional discussions during the past number of years. One very serious result has been that the federal and provincial governments together have not been nearly as diligent about confronting some of our most serious problems as they should have been. I am referring to the absence of municipal representatives from these discussions.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am not arguing that they should necessarily have the authority to attend federal-provincial conferences ex officio, but we have suffered from the fact that they have not really been able to take part in the discussions at any level. It is my hope, and the hope of those who sit with me in this House, that the parliamentary committee will provide for the representatives of our cities, towns and counties precisely that forum and that public platform which has been denied to them through the past quarter century with regard to this matter. Indeed, I would go somewhat further and suggest that if the committee is to have some resource people to help it, it should consider consulting the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities in the course of selecting some of its personnel, because I think it is only in this way that our
Canadian Constitution
members of Parliament can be assured that the interests of both the great metropolitan centres and the bustling frontier communities are properly taken into account.
All this will not be possible if the government adopts toward this committee a narrow, partisan approach. Individual members of the committee ought to have the maximum freedom to consider and discuss ideas, to present their own ideas and to convince each other of the merit of these ideas. Let us keep the whips away and, if I may say so without offence, let us all agree that this is no place for the sometimes hamhanded interference of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald).
I think the committee should be representative in every sense of the regions and the people of the country. There should be a co-chairman representing the official languages, and I think consideration should be given to one of the co-chairmen being a member of one of the opposition parties.
The terms of reference and their interpretation must not be restrictive. The wording of this resolution is a little curious, but I think that is mainly because of its parentage rather than for any other reason. It is a vast improvement over the first draft that I saw on Friday which seemed to have the effect of confining the committee to the consideration of matters that have already been proclaimed by the federal government. This would have had the effect of preventing this committee from considering on its own the proper way to approach constitutional matters. It would seem to confine the committee to staying in locked-step with discussions at federal-provincial conferences. As I see it, this defect has been removed, and the resolution that is now before us would permit the committee to consider all matters which the federal and provincial governments agreed to discuss as constitutional matters back in 1968, which, I believe, includes just about anything that one is likely to want to discuss.
It is certain that this committee must consider its method of approach to constitutional matters. It may very well decide that the method chosen by the Prime Minister and the government, and outlined by the Prime Minister this afternoon, is not working and that another method of approach, perhaps one quite substantially different, might well produce results.
The Prime Minister has said that the role of the committee is to review and judge the job which, in effect, the government of

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
Canada has been doing with regard to constitutional review. I would put it differently. I think the job of this committee is to review what has happened in connection with constitutional review, but also to decide what is the best method of proceeding with constitutional review and what method is most likely to produce the results that we want in this country.
If there is any doubt about the interpretation of the motion or about the ability, capacity or authority of this committee, then I would certainly want it corrected because it must be admitted that the approach taken by the federal government and imposed on federal-provincial conferences has so far been a failure. If there has been any progress, it is hardly measurable. The Prime Minister referred to this when he said that discussions had commenced with an outline of the program concerning human rights. As the Prime Minister has reminded us, the government put this forward as a measure for uniting rather than dividing Canadians. Yet, last December the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) had to report to the federal-provincial conference that there was no progress, or, to put it more accurately, he had no progress to report after almost two years of discussion.
In the spring of 1968, the federal government brought down, practically on tablets of stone, its white paper on international relations. I felt that that white paper was somewhat over-simplified and ignored some of our history, but certainly on the basis of that, no progress at all has been made toward the solution of one of our long standing constitutional problems. I refer to the question of how it would be possible for us in this country to sign treaties which involve, in whole or in part, implementation by provincial legislatures. There has been no progress in this regard. The whole matter seems to have become a contest between the government of Canada and the province of Quebec. This does not seem to have been resolved, either. Certainly, there has been no progress in filling in some of the great gaps in our constitution regarding matters of great importance such as, for example, the right to sign treaties involving implementation by provincial legislatures.
The white paper seems to be rather useless with regard to any of the policies of the federal government, which so far it has been unable to enforce. Indeed, I am a little puzzled about this whole thing because on reading some of the Prime Minister's earlier works I

noticed that he quoted with approval F. A. Angers. This is what he wrote:

The late Angus L. Macdonald, the distinguished former Premier of Nova Scotia and federal cabinet minister, advocated some form of delegation as a means of overcoming certain problems in our federal system. Twice in

the last decade, the federal and provincial governments have virtually reached agreement on the principle, although not on the details. I think the committee should address itself to this question.
The Hon. Walter Weir, at a federal-provincial conference in February, 1969, put forward a formula in some detail which contained five classifications of legislative power. It made some provision for a delegation. This is an approach that should be considered, with the power of delegation being clearly defined and restricted. I ask the House and the committee which this House will appoint to bear in my mind that we do not have all the time in the world to arrive at some workable arrangement.
The Prime Minister spoke about the length of the process, but the situation in Canada today is such that the people across Canada are becoming increasingly impatient and frustrated by the apparent preoccupation of the federal government with constitutional questions. The Prime Minister may think this is not exactly fair and perhaps it is not. The Prime Minister recognizes that the government appears to have a constitutional hang-up and Canadians are becoming fed up with this. On the other hand, if the situation in Quebec has not deteriorated it certainly has not improved in the last year or two. The people of Canada want to see an end to this constitutional deadlock, a break in the logjam, so that they can have answers to their questions and action on their problems.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that nothing is much easier than announcing a policy that is uncompromising, immutable and utterly irreconcilable with other points of view. Nothing is easier and more popular at certain times, but countries survive and grow, just as families get along together, by way of adjustment and honourable accommodation. Far from being a sign of weakness, honourable accommodation is the most successful and civilized kind of leadership. It serves to reconcile and unite rather than polarize or devise. It serves to overcome pettiness, suspicion and animosity. Successful and honourable accommodation and compromise summon from the people of a country, as is required from members of a family, the best of tolerance, generosity and understanding that is in them.

New developments in society cry out for a revision of the distribution of powers and responsibilities in our country and for a fresh consideration of the fiscal capacities of the several levels of government. This is known to everyone; I am not being original when I say this. I would remind the House that the powers now given to the provinces and municipalities, as well as the magnitude of expenditures, cannot be exercised or carried out by them. The burden is too great for them unless there is some kind of federal participation on an effective and substantial scale.
Everybody talks about urbanization and the effects of urbanization. The fact is that this is the source of the demand for a review of the constitution. Canada today is no longer what it was in 1867, a country with a small population the greater part of which was rural, a country in which education was merely a luxury for those who could afford it, a country where health was something to be left to God and the environment, because little else could be done about it. We are no longer that kind of country. Seventy per cent of our people are now living in urban areas and by 1980, 80 per cent will do so. All the problems the Prime Minister mentioned this afternoon, urban transportation, housing, urban renewal, recreation-particularly for the children in these huge agglomerations of high-rise apartments and choking streets-pollution and so on, have descended upon our society and will become more evident as we continue. Many of them do not recognize provincial boundaries-water pollution is one example. Many of them are beyond solution by local people, whether their representatives be municipal or provincial. What is required is the kind of national approach which the present government has refused to take, as I shall show in the course of the next few minutes. This is another reason why the need to reconsider the powers of the various levels of government and the financial capacities of those various levels became essential in the 'sixties and remains so in the 'seventies.
Another development in our society which made it necessary to examine our set-up and try to find ways of improving confederation is the tendency-one which perhaps my hon. friends and I welcome more than others in this House-for an increasing degree of government intervention in the economy, and toward an increasing provision of welfare and the benefits of a good society to our people. Whether they welcome this or not, I am sure

hon. members in all parts of the House recognize this tendency. We feel, moreover, an obligation to continue collectively to provide for the welfare of the people of Canada. This has involved a much larger degree of participation by government at all levels in the development of the country and in bringing costly amenities of life to our people. It has involved, particularly at the federal level, a search for means whereby these obligations of government in a modern society can be fulfilled.
There is a fourth development which has demanded an examination of our constitutional set-up. There is ever-increasing acceptance by people of all parties that there is a collective responsibility to achieve equality not only of opportunity but also of condition for all people in all areas, and not merely in one's own country but all over the world. This was not accepted years ago. When I first became active politically some decades ago in Montreal, I recall having to debate with people who held that if we provided unemployment insurance it would simply make people lazy; that if we gave them pensions it would destroy their souls; that if they walked in shoes with holes in the soles they were great people because they could be proud of the fact that the holes were their own. This was the attitude taken not only in Canada but in societies all over the world.
It has now been discarded, and increasingly people all over the country are demanding that governments in Canada should provide greater equality for all our citizens from coast to coast. The difficulty which arises is: how can all this be achieved; which level of government can best provide for bringing about equality of condition as between the people of Newfoundland, Ontario and British Columbia; which level of government has the means, the authority and the fiscal capacity to bring about the economic, cultural and educational development of any area? This is a pre-condition for giving the people in the disadvantaged areas of Canada an opportunity to hold their heads at least as high as those Canadians who, by accident of birth or by immigration, live elsewhere in our nation.
Hear, hear.

These are the reasons for reviewing the constitution, and if they are not the reasons, that review is a waste of time and a futile exercise which we ought to stop right now. It is the failure of the Prime Minister and the federal government to set before

the constitutional conferences these basic and human reasons which in my opinion have been responsible for the marketplace haggling which is a characteristic of these conferences instead of genuine co-operation among those who seek a common goal for all Canada.
The fact is that we have not made much progress at these meetings.

The constitutional conference is now entering its second year of proceedings and does not seem to have made very substantial progress. In fact, the situation tends, it seems to me, to become more serious in many fields. The problems which the conference must face are obviously complex and difficult. It is not my intention to blame anyone for this lack of progress. However, I would say that in several fields the position taken by the government and the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) reveal a lack of flexibility which puts obstacles in the way of the difficult discussions which must be carried on by the heads of governments in Canada.
To my mind, the Prime Minister's refusal, as emphasized by him this afternoon, to admit that Quebec is confronted with particular problems calling for special solutions is and will always be an insuperable obstacle to the constitutional review.
Mr. Schreyer, my colleague who is premier of Manitoba, mentioned this fact to the conference and also to newspapermen. Obviously, the whole system of shared cost programs as well as the problems concerning housing, urban renewal, pollution, manpower training and some aspects of social welfare, for which federal initiative and participation are required, are in danger. I do not mean by that that we should give in every time the Quebec government makes requests to Ottawa. I agree with the Prime Minister that Ottawa should not concede, as Quebec wants, that the federal government must never allocate funds for social security programs concerning Canadians living in that province.
Evidently, it is essential that Canadians throughout the country enjoy the services of the federal government and that they maintain direct relations with its institutions. It is therefore also important that Quebecers, just

like the citizens of other provinces, make use of Ottawa's special services, in order to judge the importance which the federal government attaches to their problems as well as to those of other Canadians.
But to insist on this basic principle in a federal state does not mean to deny some special problems and an unfaltering will to solve them by special means. It is unfortunate that another problem, bilingualism, seems to be getting worse. Two years ago, one could see real progress towards the recognition of bilingualism in Canada. Some provinces had made considerable efforts in that direction and everywhere there was a growing interest in the advantages to be derived from bilingualism, not only for greater unity but also for increased fairness and wealth in Canadian life and culture. Regretfully, linguistic quarrels and a few unfortunate events in Quebec created an unhealthy atmosphere that threatens the spread of bilingualism in the other provinces. I should like to give an example which is rather distressing for me. I was educated in Montreal in the English language, and I am aware of the rights I enjoyed, as are my friends and colleagues. Today however in the province of Quebec, people are wondering whether those rights will continue to exist in the future. Not only the extremists' position in Quebec is to be dreaded, but it seems evident that at the administrative level, the attitude of the Quebec government is making the problem worse.
The members from Quebec know, I am sure, that there is a new procedure in that province with regard to higher education. When a student graduates from a secondary school, he must attend a junior college for two years before being admitted to university where he has to study another three years in order to obtain a B.A. or B.Sc. degree.
I have learned from reliable sources that presently, there is only one English-speaking college in Quebec. Now, to be recognized, such a college must get approval from the Provincial Department of Education, and I am told that so far, they have refused to approve the creation of other English-speaking colleges.
The result, if such information is accurate, is that next fall, about 3,000 English-speaking

high school students will be unable to be admitted to a CEGEP, and consequently they will not be able to take up university studies.
This is an unfair situation unlikely to serve Quebec's or Canada's interests. [DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Let me say to him that I am not surprised at that. Let me say to him, I hope without presumption, that he is misunderstanding the attitude of the provinces and most of the writers of newspaper editorials. They are not disinterested in constitutional review. They are in despair at the failure of the federal government to deal with the problems which press upon the provinces, the municipalities and the people resident in them while this review is going on. That is the reason for their disinterest. It it not a rejection of the need to review and rewrite our constitution that our Prime Minister is witnessing. in this context, while their issues and problems mount or while Rome burns.
For example, how can the leader of any federal government expect that the provinces will look at constitutional review with open hearts and minds when right in the middle of that review they hear from spokesmen of the government, and I am not exaggerating even though I am not quoting, that as soon as it is possible the government intends to withdraw from the cost shared programs-perhaps not all of them but a good many of them? Just imagine what that means for the provinces. They are induced to come into the program because of the federal participation and then they are told, a year, three years or five years after that, the federal government is going to withdraw. It is true the government will make provisions for certain financial returns, but it intends to withdraw and from then on the responsibility will be entirely upon the provinces.

It is this attitude of the federal government I condemn, not the time they are taking or that the Prime Minister is taking in getting these conferences going because they cannot be done fast.

How can the Prime Minister expect representatives and the Prime Ministers of provinces to feel at ease and leisurely consider the many complex legal and social issues involved in constitutional revision when every one of them knows that in the large cities they have programs for urban renewal. While there has been some research done, the federal government and its minister responsible for housing sit in offices reviewing, reviewing and reviewing but obviously becoming more confused daily. The more the minister reads and the more he reviews the less he apparently knows of the problem. The provinces and municipalities sit with the Prime Minister and demand that something be done about

urban renewal in the large cities of this country, yet they are expected to come to a constitutional review in a leisurely way to sit and discuss constitutional problems as though there were not very urgent matters pressing upon them at home. What we resent and think is a betrayal of the needs of Canada and the Canadian people is that we are constantly being threatened by this government about our system of social security. We do not know what the result will be but we hear about task forces investigating the total system of social security and reporting. We hear statements from the government about the need for selectivity instead of universality. I am certain that every representative of every province in this country is wondering what this means for the various programs which the people in the provinces enjoy and which they share in many cases with the federal government.

This has not narrowed. How can any Prime Minister representing a province in dire need like the Atlantic provinces are, and like the province of Manitoba is to some extent, come to the table and sit with the federal government in a leisurely manner discussing the social and legal implications of constitutional review?
These are the problems that make constitutional review appear irrelevant to the representatives of the provincial governments. These are the problems that make the constitutional review misunderstood and perhaps irrelevant to the people of Canada. These are the problems that make the constitutional review irrelevant to so many people in the province of Quebec. I say to the Prime Minister and the federal government that if they are serious about the unity of this country, and serious about building a new constitution as the basis for that unity, they have to tackle these problems immediately, with some verve, some imagination, some heart and some generosity.
Canadian Constitution
I say that history is full of examples that when people sit down to write a document, a constitution, an agreement, a contract or whatever it may be for something in the future while they ignore or appear to ignore the problems that choke the people at present, the documents are not going to be written or if they are written are not going to be any good, and to the extent that they are any good, will not be worth the paper they are written on because underneath them will remain social bitterness and social misunderstanding and a great deal of regional resentment that will not allow any constitution to work.
The solution is not easy. This cannot be done overnight, but I say that the solution to the constitutional problem of Canada will not be found by merely writing a new constitution and not by merely modernizing the division of powers, but it must be based in my view and the view of my colleagues-I am sure I speak for them-on action now by the Parliament and the Government of Canada on the problems I have indicated and the many more that are well known to the Prime Minister. This should be done while this constitutional review is being carried on so that the representatives of the provinces will be sitting down with a federal government which recognizes these problems and is doing something about them. They will then, perhaps, see a better future for the citizens of the provinces and will then be willing to discuss constitutional review in a much better mood than is now the case.
I am not going to attempt to give a blueprint of the kind of thing that the committee ought to discuss because I do not think this is the purpose of this debate today. We support the setting up of this committee not only because it will enable members of opposition parties to participate in discussions on changing the constitution, but even more important, as far as I am concerned, this is the only way in which the people of Canada, through their various organizations, can be heard on the subject of constitutional change.
I am not saying this in terms intending to belittle anyone of the provinces or anyone of the governments, but you sit at these constitutional conferences and watch 11 men who have been thrown up by the accident of election with the duty and the obligation-

You better amend that
now.

January 26. 1970
Canadian Constitution

I am not amending it. This applies to my friend Mr. Schreyer as it does to the Prime Minister of Canada. By the accident of election 11 men, some with one view of Canada and some with another, some thinking they are Gods and some thinking they are demi-Gods, but no one less than that, sit there settling the future of my country. These may be the people in Canada to do it, but all of us will have some doubt about some one in that group of 11.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Particularly one.

I do not know what the alternative is. There probably is none, but as I said there is a serious question about 11 men who are there by accident of election-11 men, no more. It is true there is a cabinet, but essentially the present system means that it is the Prime Minister who settles the constitution and the future for all the people of Canada. By this means I feel there is no opportunity, except in an election or in elections, for the people of Canada to express themselves and to take part in the process of constitutional discussion and constitutional change. This is the reason we, like members of the official opposition, asked a long time ago for a parliamentary committee. If I remember correctly, my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) asked for this back in 1966 when the present Prime Minister was minister of justice, and at the time the justice minister rejected it as he later rejected the request of opposition members.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he was wrong. It may be that the Prime Minister and the premiers, 11 of them, sitting in the constitutional conferences might have behaved differently than they have behaved if the people of Canada had been given an opportunity to appear before parliamentary and legislative committees across the country and have their say about Canada and its future instead of leaving it only to the Prime Ministers. This committee will provide an opportunity for appearances by the Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, the Canadian Labour Congress-
The CM A.

The CMA, if that association has anything to say and the Canadian Bar Association if it has anything to say that concerns the welfare of the people of Canada. All these organizations and many others will

have an opportunity to appear before us and participate in this historic event.
We in this party object-and we so informed the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald)-to a joint committee on which the Senate is represented. Personally, I love every Senator individually but do not want to sit with them on any committee such as this despite my love for them individually. Aside from our opposition to the Senate as an institution in this Parliament there is another reason why in this case I object to a joint committee. I do not intend to move an amendment in this regard but I wish to place this on the record. They were not elected by the people. They do not represent the people of Canada. They were appointed by some prime ministers over the years. Many of them are defeated candidates.
Whom are the members of the CMA elected by?
They at least represent the doctors. If you want the Senators to appear before the committee to present their case for the Senate, we will hear them.
Hear, hear.

It is their presence on this committee to which we object. However, I shall not say any more about that. In any case, my time I believe is about up.
The second point I wish to make is that made by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I am probably wrong, but I was under the impression that an earlier draft of the motion contained in it a provision giving the committee permission to hire counsel and other experts. I regret very much the omission of such a provision and I hope, after the committee is established and meets, that it will come back to the House of Commons and request and receive authority to hire whatever experts and whatever assistants members of the committee may think necessary.
