Some others of my colleagues will speak in this debate and will indicate some things we believe might be done immediately, such as the inclusion of a provision for delegation of power which might solve present problems without the necessity of waiting for the total revision of the constitution.
Since the clock tells me I must, 1 shall conclude by saying this not very original thing to the House. I agree with the Prime Minister that countries and nations are not,
January 26, 1970

Canadian Constitution
despite what some people think, ordained by God and are not the result of any tablet from Mount Sinai. They are the historical development resulting from many things which it is difficult to indicate. When I wrote an article for a Canadian magazine about three years ago I said, when in certain circumstances I was asked why I was going back to Canada after I had finished my studies elsewhere, that this is rather difficult to answer and that I can only say, like Gertrude Stein, my country, my country is my country. But it is a great country; it is a tremendous country; it is a beautiful country. It is a country which has great riches underground, in the forests and in the waters. It has a great people, not greater than any other but just as great as any other people in the world.
We have the possibility of building a model society for the peoples of the world to see. We have a duty to build it because we have the resources with which to build such a society. The leaders of governments in Canada will go down in history as destroyers of human hopes if they do not succeed in this constitutional revision. The people of Canada will never forgive them if the result of this revision is not a better constitution serving the interests of the people of Canada, and indeed of the people of the world, better than our constitution has served us until now, although it has served us. As has been said, historically we face an important task. I hope and pray we are able to fulfil it with distinction and with justice to the people of our country.
Hear, hear.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher)- Post Office-assignment of new productivity executive; the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr.	Orlikow)-Manpower-adult
retraining and educational programs-alleged wasting of money; the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding)-Pollution- dumping of oil and other waste in Great Lakes.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to say a few words this afternoon on the motion introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for the setting up of a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to study the constitution and amend it slightly if need be.
Under the circumstances, we support the appointment of that committee which will enable us, first of all, to update our constitution, which is over 100 years old with a view to improving it and repatriating it, patching it up or renewing it if necessary. Indeed, that agreement has too often been bandied around by federal administrations which could not see beyond their centralist limits.
Today, when he came to the house, the Prime Minister did not agree with the constitutional review. He finally reconsidered his decision, and I congratulate him on it, and

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
allowed the creation of the present committee to study our constitution.
This review will be most fruitful at the coming federal-provincial conferences. I am convinced that it will depoliticize the conferences and encourage various groups, and even some responsible individuals, to give up their personal concepts and adapt themselves to the aspirations of the majority. Finally, it will enable us, members of this House, as well as all other responsible people at the provincial level, to hear opinions other than those of our respective governments and, for once, to have views from Canada as a whole.
One must not be afraid to face reality squarely, to find out why some provinces interpret the constitution differently. For instance, why should I, as a Quebecer, fight for ideas which some of my colleagues do not share?
To review briefly the history of the constitution, Mr. Speaker, allow me to go back to 1867, the year it was born. In 1867, Canada comprised Upper and Lower Canada. The constitution was drawn up merely in an attempt to do justice, on the one hand, to Lower Canada which was mostly made up of French Canadians settled on an area larger than present-day Quebec and, on the other hand, to Upper Canada, which territory was mostly occupied by English-speaking people.
When I hear the Prime Minister say that Quebec may not claim any more than the other provinces, I simply do not agree. Had Quebec, as a province, not been different from the others, the present constitution would have been entirely different; it might even never have existed.
History teaches us that our constitution owes its origin to the existence of Quebec. In fact, without the French Canadians in Lower Canada this country today would be administered by a single government, and there would be no need for Confederation.
Under that agreement, the provinces concerned agreed to form a central government, whereas up to then, every one of them had managed to administer itself. It must be kept in mind that the federal government owes its power to the provinces.
The numerous quarrels we have had for so many years are due to the fact that federal governments believed they had founded the provinces. We will achieve Canadian unity only if those provinces remain strong, with free government that respect the union, and only if the central government respects that agreement in order to facilitate its negotia-

tions with each of the provinces and to be able to take more effective action in areas of national interest.
I said at the outset that the Prime Minister first opposed a review of the constitution, contending that the present one was adequate to enable the Canadian people to live in harmony. I do not disapprove altogether of his idea because regardless of the snags it ran into, our constitution adequately safeguards the rights of the provinces.
Of course, the central government is highly responsible for those snags which could have probably been avoided had it co-operated more with the provinces instead of always trying to play cat and mouse with them.
In the field of taxation, what has been done? The provincial fields of jurisdiction were first encroached upon and if this continues, some day they will be taken over by the federal government at the individual, municipality and school board levels.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We oppose precisely this evolution, we of the province of Quebec, just as the citizens of other provinces should oppose it. In view of the feelings in some provinces, they remain indifferent because they profit by this attitude, while we, in the province of Quebec, have to fight against this new invasion of our provincial rights. Besides, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, as long as it is not understood that Quebec has requirements that are different from those of other provinces, we shall say that Quebec cannot give up in order to administer and to do justice to its people. We shall hold on until the end in order to stop this process.
During the study in committee, we will have surprises. Some Quebecers will come and testify impartially without indulging in politics or sentimentality, to speak frankly, like Canadians. I know that several other provinces, as mentioned by the previous speaker, are ready to recognize that Quebec has certainly got something that other provinces have not. This must be well understood.
The constitution was made because of Quebec. Quebec has its Civil Code and the other provinces their common law. It is not the same thing at all.
I could enumerate many other things. We are not like the others in Canada but this does not prevent us from being good and perfect Canadians. However-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Will the hon. member allow me a question?
January 26, 1970
Certainly.

Does the hon. member
assume that the members elected in Quebec are unable to represent and speak for this province in the same way as the members elected in other provinces speak on behalf of those provinces?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question put by the Prime Minister. It is indeed possible to represent the interests of one's province and I am here to do so. I sought election in order, to better defend the interests of my province, but in an orderly way.
People come and say that Quebec cannot manage its own administration. We are confronted with a problem: it has to be solved. Taxing powers are not evenly distributed. The federal government is boasting of surpluses and the provinces are registering deficits. The balance should be restored and this, in my opinion, should be done at the committee level. Why is the balance upset? It is because of the intrusions of the federal government in the fields coming under provincial jurisdiction.
There have been all sorts of reasons given for that. War, for instance. War was given as an excuse for encroaching upon three provincial fields of taxation: real estate tax, personal and corporation income tax and estate tax. The federal government maintained that these steps were unavoidable.
It was but an excuse, for the problems were solved through some other means. It was just an excuse to trespass on the provincial jurisdictions in order to get hold of the money in Quebec.
They promised, however, to return it as soon as the war would be over. The war has been over for a long time now but the money has still not been wholly returned. It is taking a long time and meanwhile the federal government goes on collecting money in the provinces. That is how the provinces have been deprived of their three main sources of income.
What can the provinces do in the meantime? They lack money. They also have a right to develop, as pointed out by the Prime Minister and other members. The provinces must keep pace with progress, and for that purpose, they need money which they do not have. The power to accumulate capital for administration purposes was taken away from them and they could not get it back, in spite of promises to that effect.
Canadian Constitution
That is not what the provinces need, and especially Quebec. Quebec should be allowed-and it has this right-to raise the money it needs to survive, instead of getting it from a third party.
There lies the greatest cause of injustice. Today, the same system is still being implemented. Full powers of taxation are enjoyed and all the money required is sought in the provinces.
It is wished to establish an industrial development committee. I am very happy about it. Under the circumstances, we cannot have the whole loaf, only crumbs. The establishment of this committee will enable the federal government to give something to provinces. Therefore, the provinces will obtain money tc promote education and to give assistance to the municipalities, the school boards and ever to individuals.
However, if you consider the whole issue closely, you find it is a dangerous infringement on the part of the federal government in fields coming under provincial jurisdiction.
Why? Because the federal government has all the necessary authority to lay hands on the money earned by the workers in the various provinces and to distribute it like a good father. This is not what the provinces want. They no longer want a federal government which interferes in the fields of provincial j urisdiction.
The committee should recommend that the federal government let the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction in matters coming under their competence, while granting them the rights corresponding to their duties. Are not, health, road safety and education within the competence of the provinces?
Let us give the provinces the means to raise the money required to administer, for instance, the areas connected with health or education in the province of Quebec. Then there will be peace and the province of Quebec will have the money required to cope with the situation in the areas of education or health. Thus the province of Quebec would not always have to beg the central government in order to obtain what the latter has hypocritically stolen from that province.
It was a hypocritical agreement that was entered into during the last war. The province of Quebec had been promised that its powers of taxation would be handed over right after the war. That was a piece of hypocrisy.

January 2S, 1970
Canadian Constitution
Today, the money required to administer the province of Quebec is still taken away from the workers. Some seem astonished-in a hypocritical way-that the Quebec government is clamouring for its revenues. What a joke!
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
First you take away a man's clothes, throw him naked on the street, then have the police arrest him because he has nothing on. Such is the situation of the province of Quebec, to whom they say: you need our help because you cannot administer some of your departments. But what do they do? They simply hand over to the province the money which already belongs to it. The committee should finally be able to understand the situation.
I went out West, and I met honest people there. I had talks with them and I believe life would be more worthwhile if rights were respected.
Mr. Speaker, is it conceivable that the municipality should tell the father, the wage-earner: "Turn your salary over to me and I will give you as much as I please. You will eat what I choose."?
Yet that is what is taking place between the federal government and the provinces. Little wonder that Quebec is in a turmoil, and we have not seen anything yet. If the federal government does not put a stop to this thrust, I cannot answer for anything in Quebec, a province well known to me because I travel through it all year long. And let nobody think that only a small minority of 3 or 4 per cent is involved.
The unrest brought about by all this disunion today is due to the hypocritical interference of the federal government in Quebec. Having been stripped, the citizen is covered with a piece of cloth and told: "You're lucky!
I am honest and generous since I cover you with a cloth". That is not what Quebec wants. It simply wants to recover its taxation rights, in order to give its people what they need in the fields coming under its jurisdiction.
I do not know if this is clear enough and if I can be understood today by most members. I am so anxious that this review prove useful. I hope my words can convince some sincere members from the other provinces. I do not think any member would purposely do wrong. If he does, it would be because he is misinformed.
The problem has never been put properly. We have had to learn false histories of Canada and now we are being told false eco-
nomic stories. As I said at the outset, we must face the facts if we want to do constructive work in committee. If we Canadians want to get along with each other and cooperate. I am sure we shall have made a first step towards Canadian unity.
The policy of the federal government in the western provinces has been clearly explained, and the citizens have understood. We do not wish to take anything away from anybody, but we want at least to be allowed to keep what we have to live, like all other Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, had I known that I was going to speak today, I would have prepared my speech and would have been able to make a clearer presentation. I may however have that opportunity if I am appointed to the committee, although I am already sitting on some others.
I am confident that the members of the committee will get to the grass-roots and will discuss the matter without bias. If, for once, this is done within the committee whose sole aim would be to ensure Canadian unity, then the committee will be doing a good job.
It is essential that this review be made democratically and that the witnesses, wherever they come from, be heard with an open mind. The report of the committee should be submitted to the provinces, so that they may be in a position to discuss the future of the country without forgetting that the main point to be considered is national unity.
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked my intervention this afternoon to be better prepared, but we do not control the circumstances. I hope that my comments will lead hon. members towards this unity we are all hoping for. Let us co-operate to reach that common goal and everyone of us should apply his intelligence and his goodwill to that task.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Is the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson) rising to ask a question?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) would permit a question. In transferring taxing powers to the federal government, in the opinion of the hon. member did the province of Quebec lose more than any other province of Canada?
January 26, 1970

Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can answer the hon. member who wanted to know whether Quebec had endured greater losses than another province in the adventure of Confederation. Even if I tried to do so, I would not have all the statistics. I told the House about the principle of taxation. Those who work want only one thing: to get their pay directly at the end of the week and not through a third party.
Provincial governments have responsibilities to which correspond the right of access to three taxation fields which hopefully will be given back to the province of Quebec, provided it is willing to deal with them. It must be recognized once and for all that Quebec has that right.

Mr. Speaker, when this motion was put on the Order Paper I had high hopes that the debate would be a departure from the federal-provincial discussions on the constitution. I hoped that, perhaps by co-operation among members of the House, we might be able to break the deadlock that has taken place in federal-provincial conferences and reach a consensus as members of different parties. I hoped this would be done in a nonpartisan way. I still hope we can do this and that we can make a real contribution in this respect.
However, this afternoon I was a bit disappointed, and that is why I just said that I hoped all these things would be done. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) rose to speak, he also said he would be nonpartisan, then immediately made derogatory remarks about the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and questioned the order in which the agendas had been drawn up. He wanted to know why the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had not dealt first with the problems of the cities instead of with welfare. I found all this a little picayune. I suppose if we had started with the cities, we would have been accused of not starting with welfare. The fact is that from the very beginning the Government of Canada under the former Prime Minister set out a program of action for these federal-provincial conferences.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
All the proposals of the government have been set out quite clearly in the constitutional booklets. The first booklet dealt in a general way with the proposals for constitutional
Canadian Constitution
reform and the sociological and political implications that were necessary for making the changes. The next booklet dealt with the charter of human rights. Other booklets are entitled, "The Constitution and the People of Canada", "The Federal-Provincial Spending Power", "The Taxing Powers of the Constitution" and "Federalism and International Relations". We then went into the division of powers. The first matter dealt with in the division of powers was welfare and income maintenance.
I hope the parliamentary committee, comprised of members of all parties, will co-operate in developing a consensus on the Canadian Constitution and will break the deadlock that has taken place in the federal-provincial meetings. I agree this committee may be able to do th'ngs that the federal-provincial conference has not been able to do, because we have not only representatives of the four parties in the House but representatives of the different regions in Canada in a way the government does not. The Conservatives have strong representation from the Maritimes and the Prairies. The Creditistes have strong representation from rural Quebec. The New Democrat'c Party has representation from the Prairies as well as some of the cities. I am optimistic; I think we can work to accomplish something that will bring about a constitution befitting this great country of ours.
In addition to the usual witnesses from the intermediary bodies, trade unions, the CMA and other groups that have been mentioned, I hope we will meet members of the legislative assemblies of the provinces, not only government members but opposition members. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that we should meet representatives of the cities either through citizens' associations or the city councils. A committee of this House did hear the chairman of the executive committee of the city of Montreal when we were dealing with the Company of Young Canadians.
I think it would be well for us to hear the representations of the cities in this matter. I believe now is a good time for us to take this initiative. We cannot be dogmatic in this regard. Perhaps it should have been done before, or maybe it should be done later. In any case, we are doing it now and this is a good time because frustration is building up among some Canadians because of the lack of progress resulting from the constitutional conference. It appears to them the conference is not resolving anything.

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
As the Prime Minister pointed out, the provinces which started this process to a great extent have not put forward their proposals in the same precise manner as the Government of Canada. An exception to this is the province of Quebec, which had an allparty committee of its legislative assembly. The province of Quebec put forward specific proposals, but the other provinces have not been so specific. They have discussed the proposals but have not replied specifically to them. Some provinces have from time to time tried to act as broker between the federal government and the government of Quebec, but they have not spoken in specific terms in the same way as the federal government in its seven constitutional papers which have been very specific on the points put forward for discussion today.
Many people, in their frustration, are beginning to say they have had enough of this constitutional discussion and we should get down to discussing some of the problems of Canada which have a higher priority, such as pollution, inflation and the problems of the cities. When dealing with problems such as those I have just mentioned, we must not forget that they are very much related to the constitution. Very often we cannot act in the way we would like to act, because of the constitution. This is natural. The constitution was drafted 100 years ago at a time when technology had not developed to the extent it has today. These problems have grown up around a new technology and new type of society. The legislative categories in the constitution are just not adequate.
We have been successful in doing some of these things through co-operative federalism. This process of co-operative federalism originated in the United States and we have used it for the last ten years. Problems do not fit easily into categories of legislation. No matter how perfect a constitution, if we are to do a good job it is obvious that all levels of government must co-operate and use their different areas of jurisdiction to deal adequately with problems.
Unfortunately, the division of power under our constitution is in many respects out of date. This matter is under review to help us deal with problems more expeditiously and with greater vigour. I do not think it can be said that we have not acted in areas where we have jurisdiction, nor that we have not taken initiatives where the jurisdiction is not clear. An example of that is the Water Act. One might argue that the jurisdiction in this area is not clear, yet the federal government,

following the Resources for Tomorrow Conference, took the initiative and tried to do something about a very real problem. No matter how perfectly we set up these divisions of power and categories for legislative competence, we will still need a spirit of cooperation, a creative federalism, if we are to have a smoothly-run country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, immediately before supper I was discussing the division of power under the present constitution and I said that the powers which the federal government and the provincial governments now exercise are not adequate to meet the technical and social realities of 1970.
It seems to me that under the present constitution legislative powers are too inflexible and too exclusive. In my view it would be better if we made greater use of concurrent powers such as those now used in respect of agriculture, immigration and pensions. These powers belong to both levels of government, though should conflict arise the right of para-mountcy is given to one of the jurisdictions. In other words, both governments are free to legislate, but if there is conflict the constitution states which jurisdiction has paramount-cy.
A solution along these lines was put forward in the recent white paper on the constitution, dealing specifically with income maintenance. I believe that an arrangement of this kind would result in a more flexible and functional constitution. I also believe that in certain cases we should consider favourably a proposition giving one level of government the right to delegate its powers under the constitution to another level of government.
Several problems have arisen in recent years directly related to the constitutional situation. One of them has to do with conditions in our cities. Some people have criticized the federal government on the grounds that it is not concerned with the cities; that it has done nothing to legislate for them. Such statements are inaccurate. We have passed a good deal of legislation which affects the cities-measures dealing with transportation, housing, health and welfare, labour, manpower, and so on. This legislation has had a great impact on the cities. The fact is there is no
January 26, 1970

comprehensive power vested in the federal government under the present constitution which permits the federal government to legislate directly for the cities. The comprehensive powers under section 92 of the BNA Act belong to the provinces.
If we were to legislate unilaterally in a comprehensive way, we would be violating the present constitution and, moreover, doing so at the very time we are trying to negotiate a new constitution with a new division of powers. Were we to take such a course, our proposals at these constitutional conferences would simply not be credible. We cannot legislate unilaterally in areas which belong to the provinces, while supporting an entirely different principle at constitutional conferences. Again, such a course might be taken as a licence to the provinces to intervene in areas which are specifically federal.
This leads us to the field of external affairs. Some provinces have been seeking to conclude agreements with other countries with regard to matters over which they say they have jurisdiction. Nevertheless, as has been well set out in the white paper dealing with international relations as they concern the constitution, if this were permitted, unfortunate consequences might follow. For example, Canada might be following a general foreign policy with respect to, say, Rhodesia or South Africa which included a boycott. At the same time, a province might decide to carry on a teacher-exchange program or an apprentice training program in co-operation with the country concerned, stating that such arrangements fall within the jurisdiction of its department of education or department of labour.
It is evident that the federal government cannot permit arrangements of this kind. Even in areas of provincial jurisdiction, relations outside Canada must be carried on under the umbrella of the federal government. It seems this question is coming to the fore once again: over the weekend it appears there has been a breakdown of the entente between Ottawa and Quebec with respect to this sphere of responsibility. I think the federal government will have to adopt a much tougher attitude in respect of intrusions by the provinces into this area of jurisdiction. Certain sanctions will have to be imposed.
The federal government will have to put its foot down if Quebec or any other province continues to intervene in external affairs. I would go so far as to say we should revoke the Canadian passports of individuals who
Canadian Constitution
blatantly disregard federal jurisdiction in this field. We should refuse visas to officials of foreign countries who wish to come to Canada under arrangements of which the federal government does not approve. If necessary, we should sever diplomatic relations with the countries concerned. In fact, it will probably not be necessary to do these things but we should let it be known that this is the type of sanction which the federal government has power to exercise. Let us make it clear that while we intend to respect provincial areas of jurisdiction, we do not intend to allow them to intrude into federal fields; we shall try to negotiate these matters with the provinces, but if they insist on intruding into federal fields of jurisdiction, sanctions will be brought to bear.
There are other items I should like to discuss, one of which was referred to by a speaker from the New Democratic Party. He mentioned the frustration expressed by the Premier of Manitoba at the close of the last federal-provincial conference. The premier stated in an interview that Quebec had a special set of problems which called for special arrangements. When asked whether it needed a special status, Premier Schreyer replied, "Those are not my words. I said 'special arrangements' ", Well, some have stated there have always been special arrangements for Quebec and for other provinces, too. That is true, Mr. Speaker, but these special arrangements have not been in the area of legislative powers.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
In Quebec we have the Civil Code; we have special arrangements with respect to French education and English education. There has always been the right of using the two languages in the legislature. There have been other special arrangements which apply to the province of Quebec, but there have been no special legislative powers which Quebec has and which, for other provinces, belong to the federal government.
It is all right to suggest special arrangements, but I do not think we can expect that one province will have the power to legislate in certain areas that, for other provinces, come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. If we do that, as has been suggested many times by the Prime Minister we may end up with a situation where a great many members of this House will not have the same power as other members who sit here. Special arrangements, yes-and let us

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
be specific about those special arrangements- but special powers, no.
There has been quite a bit of discussion with respect to the proposed charter of human rights, and as an English-speaking person from the province of Quebec I see a great need for this particular item, especially because of what happened in St. Leonard and what might happen in other parts of Quebec. I think we must be certain that our civil liberties are protected in a way which cannot be derogated from or taken away by the federal government, provincial governments, municipal governments or school boards. I believe that they should be protected in the constitution through a Bill of Rights or in some other way which would require special legislative power to effect their change.
I do not accept the argument of those who say these rights are protected by the courts. They have not been protected by the courts. If we had such a charter of civil liberties, the people of St. Leonard would not have had their right to education or language taken [DOT]away from them, and many years ago the people of Manitoba might not have had their right to education in French taken away from them.
With respect to the proposals relating to a special or revised Supreme Court of Canada, I Relieve it is extremely important that we have one section of the Supreme Court to deal with civil law cases coming from the province of Quebec, and that civil law cases are not decided by judges trained in the common law. Having practised in that area of law for many years, I can understand how a court dominated by common law judges can often twist the civil law or put an interpretation on it which a civil law judge would not.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is one area that has not been discussed and which we must consider for constitutional change, and that is the House of Commons itself. Last year we made a lot of changes with respect to rules of the House, but in my view there are many other problems which will have to be dealt with in a constitutional way.
We talk about whether this Parliament and the House of Commons are really relevant to the demands of the day. In many ways I do not think the House is relevant to those demands. I think the only way we can make it relevant is to change its constitutionality. Mr. Speaker, some of these suggestions have already been put forward. I do not think they suggest we are going to the republican
[Mr. Allmand.l
system, but they borrow some things from that system. For example, I feel we should have a set period for a Parliament, a four-year period or a five-year period. The government would continue in office during that period whether or not its legislation was defeated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am afraid his time has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in 20 minutes there is not too much that can be said about the constitution but I would make some statements which may be of some use at this time. Following the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. All-mand), I have just one or two comments to make about his speech. He said something about changing the House of Commons constitutionally. I, of course, would point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is trying to change it constitutionally.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He is doing his best to sterilize it at the present time. The hon. member also said something about concurrent powers, and he particularly mentioned agriculture. As I look opposite and see the amiable and distinguished Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), I think that while he is operating only under concurrent powers he has made such a mess of trying to do things for the people of western Canada that he could not do any worse even if he had full power. Therefore, I do not see that concurrent power would really be of any assistance.
I am very interested in this motion, Mr. Speaker, because about five years ago I put on the Order Paper a private member's notice of motion along very much the same lines. I went a little further with mine. I think that one or two years later the motion was put on behalf of this party. I was fortunate in the draw, and we had quite an interesting debate on this issue. This was in 1965 or 1966.
I proposed the establishment of a committee of this kind because I believed then, as I more strongly believe now, that only through a mechanism of this kind can we bring before the people of Canada, in a simplified way, the extremely important issues which are involved.
I was rather amused by the Prime Minister, who said everything had been very carefully planned. The right hon. gentleman indicated
January 26, 1970

that all the steps were taken one by one, all according to a deep-laid plan, and that everything was coming out just as he had anticipated. I cannot accept that for a moment.
The Prime Minister was engaging in playing a nice little game. He had his constitutional experts locked up in one little room and his economic experts locked up in another little room, and he was running from one room to the other having a great time. Suddenly the Prime Minister of Ontario called the Conference for Tomorrow, and from then on the federal government and the Prime Minister were kicked into this issue and were compelled to take steps which I do not think they had the slightest intention of taking. I do not think there was the careful preparation to which the right hon. gentleman referred. I think that is so much hogwash, Mr. Speaker-certainly the results would so indicate.
With respect to the terms of reference, this is a rather peculiarly worded motion. I hope that once the committee is functioning there will be no attempt to prevent i!s canvassing fully all the problems and all the suggested alternatives of our constitutional difficulties. I will take one minute to enlarge on this theme.
I have read the motion. It refers to the conference of February, 1968. At that time, Mr. Speaker, there was a series of subjects laid out for the continuing consideration of the constitutional conference. These subjects covered the waterfront. From that time until now this government has put forward a number of proposals, some of which I agree with and some of which I do not, dealing in one way or another with all the questions which were first outlined in the agenda and in the report made in February, 1968.
I would take it from that-and I did not understand the right hon. gentleman to indicate anything to the contrary-that when the committee is given jurisdiction in this matter after the motion has been passed, there will be no attempt to inhibit the committee from the fullest and most complete discussions.
I have said something about the various conferences which have taken place. There is no question about it-my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has made this quite plain-that there has been a complete failure so far as the conferences are concerned. I think this was almost inevitable because of the way in which they were developed. All we have had is a confrontation among adversaries, among 11 governments all
Canadian Constitution
seeking to hold the power they have within their respective establishments, and if possible to add to that power. I do not fault them on that score; I think it is perfectly natural and what one might expect of the type of conference and discussion that has taken place. But this is not good enough. We shall not get anywhere if we continue this type of meeting.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Conferences must be held, of course, to capitalize on and consolidate the gains which are made in other ways. However, to the extent to which we hoped in the past that a series of constitutional conferences of heads of government would produce workable changes and reforms in our constitution, we might just as well realize that this will never take place in that way.
What do you suggest?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the minister will wait a while, he will hear some excellent suggestions, although on the basis of our experience with agriculture I do not know that he will listen to them.
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude my remarks before my time expires. I should like to see this committee take a view that is as non-controversial and objective as possible. I do not expect that politics will not be involved. Of course they will, and that is to be expected, but I hope the hon. members who comprise that committee will approach the subject matter in a frame of mind which will be more conducive to light than to heat.
I should like to see the committee composed of members of this House and members of the other place who will travel from place to place in Canada. I do not expect we will have a repetition of the famous confederation parade which took place in 1964 and 1965, but I think we can absorb something from that. After all, this is not a means by which we are going to settle conflicts between governments immediately.
The more than 21 million people in Canada are now engaged in the process of looking at the world they live in and should be coming to a decision on how they want to rearrange the powers of government at the various levels. In the first place, it must be abundantly clear that these are simple issues. The constitution as discussed by lawyers may become quite complex, quite difficult and very learned; but there are a number of simple

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
issues which must be put to the people of Canada.
Do they desire, for example, to continue the same kinds of government in the questions involving transportation, education, trade and commerce, and so on and the new problems that have arrived on the scene regarding pollution, our cost of living and inflation? I suggest these problems will continue to be with us for many years. We must consider the problems of our Indian people. They are demanding rights which have been taken away from them. We also have problems in respect of the urban situation. As one hon. member said, 70 per cent of the people of Canada living in urban areas are seeking houses, solutions to the problem of juvenile delinquency, urban reclamation, and so on.
These are problems which have emerged. The people of Canada want to know where the jurisdiction lies and what is to be done about them. I think it is as simple as that. I hope this committee will be able to reduce these problems to simple terms. I suggest to the news media, the press, television and radio people that this will provide a magnificent opportunity for them. We will shortly be dealing with the whole issue of television and radio coverage in this chamber, in committees of the House and places in this building where the electronics media may have access to members for clarification. I hope they will be allowed to play a very important and significant role in reducing these problems to the most simple terms possible for placing before the people.
The committee will be the master of its own destiny. It will indicate what procedures it wishes to follow. I suggest that the committee give serious thought to not only permitting but encouraging radio and television production of its proceedings, so there will be available to the people of Canada an explanation of what is going on and what are the issues. In that way we will do what I think is essential. We will fulfil a condition precedent to the settling of these problems by letting the people "in" on a great national debate. In this way all the people of Canada who are interested will be able to see what issues are at stake and express their points of view. I think only in that way will we arrive at solutions.
Whether the people live in Quebec, Ontario, Peace River, Vancouver or Victoria, they are all Canadians. When the people see what is involved and how these issues have been

reduced to simple terms, they will in due course exert pressure on the respective governments to bring about answers to problems. Not too much time will elapse before that situation comes about. They will not seek the answers of the Government of Canada or the answers of the governments of Saskatchewan, Newfoundland or Quebec; they will seek the answers that they want. I suggest to the members of the committee that will be formed that this is one way in which these questions can be brought home, simply and easily, to the people of Canada in order that they may have a chance to participate. This chance has been denied them up to the present.
Let me take just a minute to deal with some of these questions. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) quite properly chastised the Prime Minister because, as he said, he was hung up on the constitution and many of the problems I have mentioned. The federal government has ample authority under the constitution to deal adequately with the serious problem of pollution. What will happen if we accept the government's position on this question? We may wait two or three years before the government comes to a conclusion, if it ever does, as to what authority it has. Only then will we consider legislation. Consider at the weak, pitiful water bill we have been debating: even the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), with his usual eloquence, was hard put to it to promote a suitable defence to the criticisms from this side of the House.
The government has jurisdiction under the Navigable Waters Protection Act which prohibits the pollution of water. It has jurisdiction under the Fisheries Act, which contains similar provisions, the Shipping Act and the Migratory Birds Convention Act. These four pieces of legislation, enacted by the federal Parliament, contain definite and categorical sanctions against the pollution of water. We are compelled to put up with this monstrosity conceived by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his colleagues.
The same thing applies to urban matters. There was a Supreme Court decision not long ago to the effect that rapid transit arrangements in large metropolitan areas are the subject of federal jurisdiction. This is true in respect of housing, and so on. For years the federal government has been involved, with no suggestion that it has been usurping a jurisdiction which belongs to the provinces. It
January 26, 1970

has been involved in these programs. There are such problems as juvenile delinquency, urban renewal and other measures related to the cities. The federal government has a very substantial measure of jurisdiction today. I am not suggesting, in breach of certain obvious rights which exist in the provincial governments, that this federal government or any federal government should rush in hamhanded and deal without consultation and co-operation with these questions. However, there is jurisdiction which can be exercised. I suggest that the right hon. gentleman, the Minister of Agriculture and their colleagues have been using the constitution as a smokescreen. They have been afraid.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are a number of areas in which the federal government has jurisdiction to act and in which it could have acted. I do not suggest it should do so without adequate consultation. At the same time, this does not mean there are not a great many areas in which the provincial governments must not only retain but to some extent change or even increase their jurisdiction.
A federal entity comes about because by reason of geography, economy, culture, race, and so on. There are natural divisions which should retain their particular identity. There is nothing wrong with that. I think all people who speak about Canada say it is a great country because it is unique in its diversity. Why should there not be diversification in so far as the provinces are concerned? British Columbia, sheltered behind the Rocky Mountains, is quite different from Alberta. Alberta and Saskatchewan, both carved out of the same rib at the same time, went different ways after a period in which their history was approximately the same. One had a government under the premiership of my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and the other had a Social Credit government. Both were as different, ideologically, as can be, but were created at the same time.
That there should be diversity is a fact. Some of us who have been involved in municipal government know that under a common municipal act there may be 20 municipalities, each operating under the same legislation but which because of the people involved and because of certain divergent and distinctive characteristics are different kinds of
Canadian Constitution
municipalities. I think I would be going contrary to the views of the political party to which I have the honour to belong if I did not say I believe in diversity individually and with regard to provincial governments, and that there should be every opportunity to continue to develop the peculiar distinctions between the different provinces of this country.
I see my time is running out, and there is so much more I should like to say. However, there is one other important item with which I shall deal. The federal government now has an opportunity to seek some redress in these constitutional problems. The Supreme Court has handed down decisions which would seem to take away some of the jurisdiction which might have belonged to provincial governments or the federal government from time to time. It may well be, in light of existing conditions, that these decisions should be different.
A recent case in the Supreme Court of Canada, Regina v. Binus, laid down, not as obiter dicta but as part of the judgment, that the principle of stare decisis did not apply. In other words, the Supreme Court of Canada can hand down a decision in constitutional cases different from that which it has handed down in the past. Over the last six or eight years it seems to me the federal government should have been reviewing some of these constitutional cases in collaboration with the provinces. Constitutional history has set governments on paths different from those intended by the Fathers of Confederation.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are growing impatient so I shall await another opportunity to make the few more comments I wanted to make.

Mr. Speaker, I think one of the most striking features that emerges in any debate on our constitution is the difference between what the constitution actually is in practice and what the people of this country believe it should provide for and what it should be. When I look over a range of national problems, I see the vast divergence between the constitution as it is and what the ordinary person in this country thinks it should be.
At this time of inflation, the average Canadian thinks the federal government should have power, if it wishes to exercise it, to control rents, prices and the cost of living. We know it does not have that power. The average Canadian thinks the federal govern-

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
ment should have greater involvement in housing and in the control of policies concerning urban planning, major labour disputes and agricultural prices.
The average Canadian increasingly in this day and age believes the federal government should have a good deal more to say about foreign intrusion into our economy. Although I do not like to disturb any sacred cows, the average Canadian of my acquaintance also believes there is and should be some federal responsibility in the field of education. I am sure I am not the only person who has constituents who moved across the length and breadth of Canada and found, each time they moved, that their children lose time in school and some became discouraged to the point that they dropped out of school altogether.
One of the serious problems we face in this country-it is not a technical or legal problem but a serious, practical one-is the difference between what our constitution in fact is and what the ordinary person thinks it should be and wishes it were. The average person is confused by the lack of connection between his idea of who should govern the country and what actually happens. He wonders why the governments of this country are paralyzed in respect of major decisions.
The average person says, and with truth, that the present system lends itself to buckpassing, to the ducking of responsibility and to a patent inability to deal quickly with major problems. I say to all of us in this honourable House that these are things we cannot ignore. They are problems which exist and with which we must be prepared to deal. We cannot deed with them in the traditional way, whereby the provinces blame the federal government for what is wrong, or vice versa, and one party lists a great number of things it thinks another party should be doing or talking about.
When we say we have a constitutional problem, believe me we should mean it, because we have. We should be prepared, together in this Parliament and indeed with all our fellow legislators across the country, to bring about some kind of solution. The confusion about the meaning of our constitution would seem to be the best possible reason for the type of public inquiry which is now envisaged by this resolution. One thing this inquiry might do, as my hon. friend just suggested, is bring the issues out in the open. It will have an educational function.
I hope, however, no one is under the illusion that it is only the public which must be

educated. It seems to me that the people who require education the most are those who represent us collectively in these dominion-provincial discussions of our constitution and other matters of joint concern. We have 11 governments, one federal and ten provincial, which meet to discuss a great variety of issues. I am sure I am not the only person who believes that perhaps they should listen more to the public and less to themselves in some of these discussions.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Who speaks for whom at these conferences? If, for example, the federal government and the province of Ontario were in conflict, which of the two would represent my constituents? Is it true that they would be represented in this conflict, if it existed, by the province of Ontario? Not always. Certainly the problem which has emerged is that the various governments, whose position is established by law, translate it into the belief that they speak for the people where any of then-interests are concerned. I say that this is not so, and what we should attempt to do in the work of this committee first and foremost, is find out what the public really think about their constitution. Surely you can make them more interested by the use of television and by all the other modem means of communication.
I think that this committee would fail in its duty if it did not go out actively to try to find out what the public think. This cannot be done by the kind of formal presentation where one interest group or another comes before the committee in a small room. Why do we not use imaginatively and definitively the means which we now have at our disposal? Let us have polls taken and surveys conducted in an attempt to ascertain the attitude of the people about their constitution and about the authority which they feel should have the main and the leading role to play in the various matters of contention between the federal government and provincial governments.
The present discussions, as many speakers have indicated, have been going on now for a period of two years, and obviously they have not taken the course that some people thought they would. My friend, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), referred today to the fact that sometimes they are like public auctions. But he knows better than I do that these discussions have less of that quality than any previous discussions among
January 26, 1970

Canadian Constitution
the federal government and provincial governments.
I am sure that some provinces came to these discussions with the belief that all they had to do was to state their terms and more money and authority would be given to them. But for once we have an honest discussion of the problems of our constitution where something is asked for by the provinces and equally something is asked for by the federal government.
There is a great need in this country to expand the federal power in many important areas of our life. I think that what has been surprising in these constitutional discussions is that they have not been what my friend referred to as a sort of public auction of the tax rights or authority of the federal government. Rather, they have turned into an honest discussion of how we can functionally rearrange our constitution to make it a more fitting instrument in this twentieth century. The discussions have been far-ranging, from a proposal to entrench a Bill of Rights, to the recreation of the Supreme Court, to treaties, and the old subject of the distribution of power between the federal government and provincial governments.
The reception that has been accorded the federal proposals is one which we should have expected. There have been a variety of responses. Some provinces like some proposals and dislike others; some political parties like some proposals and dislike others. Some people say, as has been said today, that there should be a really dramatic declaration by the federal government in these discussions, and they follow that by saying, "But we must not have a confrontation". We should not be afraid of a constitutional discussion and we should not be afraid of controversy that might develop at those constitutional discussions because they affect the future of all of us and of our country.
I would like to make one or two specific comments about the work of this committee. The first comment is one which at least the members of my profession in this House will understand. It is that it is completely beyond the range of possibility to develop a perfect constitution. Even if tonight it were possible for us in this chamber to write down in black and white, indeed in letters of gold, a constitution which would solve all the problems of this country, we know that tomorrow something would crop up somewhere which would make that constitution out of date.
The codifiers, from Justinian to Napoleon, have found out to their sorrow that one cannot legislate perfection in the law or in constitutions. Therefore, we must recognize that any constitution worthy of its name must, be one which is capable of sound application by the various levels of government and of sound interpretation by the courts.
I would like to speak for a few minutes about the application of the constitution. If I may adopt a colloquialism I would say, "Don't knock the BNA Act," because it has survived 100 pretty strenuous years. Notwithstanding all the difficulties which may have arisen in applying it, the collective good sense of the Canadian people has always prevailed in difficult situations. We have emerged from the little, rural type of country which we were 100 years ago into a great, burgeoning industrial nation-and we have the same written constitution as we had then. Any constitution, whether it was written in 1867 or is written-today, must be one that can be applied in the same way to developing circumstances and to. new conditions.
One of the great things that has happened in recent years has been the systemization of federal-provincial relations. The criticism which has been levelled at all these federal-provincial meetings, which have been so important in the recent history of our country, is that they were held in secret. That criticism can be met, or at least blunted, by the appointment of this type of committee which will throw this process open to the public view and which, I hope, will encourage all the participating governments to express their opinions openly.
In speaking about the application of our-constitution to the problems of our day, I am bold enough to make one suggestion: what one might call the major, sweeping problems facing this country can never be made the subject of the sole jurisdiction of either the provinces or the federal government. At the present time, as I have said, matters such as housing, welfare, pollution, economic growth and the like are primarily subjects under provincial jurisdiction, but really they are under the joint jurisdiction of the federal government and provincial governments.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
No matter how the constitution might be-rewritten, it is my opinion that major problems of this kind will continue to be jointly under federal and provincial jurisdiction. Therefore, we must be prepared to carry on,.

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
as we have in the last few years, in a joint approach of the federal government and provincial governments toward the application of our constitution to the major problems of Canada.
My hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), at the conclusion of his remarks spoke about the interpretation of the constitution and about the new doctrine expounded by the Supreme Court of Canada, that it is not bound by its previous decisions in every instance. In my opinion we have not used our constitution in the same dynamic, testing sense as the Americans. I think that a modern federal constitution requires to be tested in the fire; it requires to be continually used, to be expounded and used as a probe to determine where and by whom jurisdiction in new areas can be exercised. We have not done this, neither the provinces nor the federal government, to anything like the extent of the United States.
I think that in the future, no matter what has been done with the constitution, we will find it necessary to subject it more frequently to judicial interpretation. This will emphasize the role of the Supreme Court of Canada. To me this also signifies that one of the most important areas for consideration in amending the constitution is the proposal which has been made for the reconstitution of the Supreme Court on lines which will make it more acceptable to the provinces of Canada.

I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question, Mr. Speaker. We are arriving at a decade which suggests that the individual should be more important than all other things which may concern his administration. The hon. member is suggesting that the whole administration of the individual should lie within the realm of the Supreme Court of Canada. I ask for clarification on that point. Is he really suggesting that the jurisdiction of the freedom of the individual should rest solely with the Supreme Court of Canada, rather than under Parliament and the freedoms which Parliament should grant in a democracy?

Mr. Speaker, I accept the hon. gentleman's statement that that is a question. I was speaking about the interpretation of the constitution in terms of assessing the distribution of power as between the federal government and provincial governments. I was not addressing my remarks to the other, equally important question of the protection of

human rights. I have not time to deal with that matter but I can say, very briefly, that it is important and long overdue that we entrench a Bill of Rights in our constitution. I think, following the example of our neighbours to the south, that we can have every confidence that this would enhance the freedom of Canadians and more particularly is it important in an era wherein there is increasing government intervention in every aspect of the life of the community.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I should like to express some views on specifics which I think are important in dealing with the constitution. Repeating what I said at the beginning, I am concerned that in our country people expect the federal government to play a leading role, most particularly in the development of the Canada economy. I think it is quite apparent at the present time that because of our constitutional arrangements, the federal government cannot play the role it should in the development of Canada and the Canadian economy. It is true that it has wide powers- taxing power, spending power, control over currency, banking and international trade, control over transport and communications- but it is not able to exercise powers in important areas affecting the life of the citizen. It has limited powers in terms of national planning. It has, as we know, limited powers in housing, control of economic growth and to exercise, when need be, firm economic controls on inflation. As I said earlier, if there is any meaning to the questions raised about foreign intrusion into our economy, the federal government has very little power to deal with this problem. It is hampered in its approach to harmful business practices-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am afraid his time has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member be granted leave to continue his remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I merely wish to add that the federal government is hampered in its control of harmful business practices, as was pointed out in the recent report of the Economic Council.
In conclusion, may I say that the appointment of this committee is an important development in our growing knowledge of our
January 26, 1970

Canadian Constitution
constitution and the problems it creates. I hope the committee will become a positive force in indicating to not only the members of this House but to all people the scope we have to make our country operate successfully under the present constitution by agreement, by novel interpretation, by experimentation and by amendment.

Mr. Speaker, if there is a general feeling that our constitution should be examined with a view to changing it, I believe that the proper first step is to have this examination carried out by a committee of Parliament. But I remain convinced, as I was when this matter was before the House last February, that there is no urgency about this matter. Certainly it should not be given precedence in Parliament over much more pressing national problems.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) covered the waterfront in his remarks when he said that the federal government should be strengthened and the provincial governments should be strengthened. I just worry about what the citizens of this country will do.
I agree that the hon. member is correct in his assessment of the constitution, because I am also convinced that the constitution as it stands today, 103 years after its coming into effect, is quite adequate to meet the demands made upon it, no matter how complex and difficult our public affairs become. It has proved to be flexible and adaptable to a very wide range of national crises from world wars to worldwide depression.
As long as Canadian leaders and statesmen have utilized our constitution in good faith, it has proved more than adequate. Unfortunately, in recent years we have had clear evidence that even such a basically sound document as the British North America Act is not proof against the manipulation of an unscrupulous Prime Minister. Its strength lies in its use, its weakness in the fact that it can be bypassed. In my view it lacks the vital provisions that would curb the assumption of unlimited and irresponsible power by the executive.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
If we are to amend our constitution, the first and most urgent change we should make is to write into the constitution curbs on the taxing and spending powers of the federal government and the ability of the Prime Minister to ignore Parliament and the constitu-21611-41
tion. The record of the government immediately past, and of the present one, is appalling in respect of trampling on the constitution, slighting the rights of the provinces and concentrating power in the hands of the central government at Ottawa an ever larger share of total spending and total government taxation.
Taxation in this country has risen steeply until today it has reached the dangerous pinnacle of more than one-third of the gross national product. This is beyond the point which economists and historians claim it is safe for any society to go without running the risk of complete economic and social decay. We should provide a constitutional check to ensure that all governments stay within a fair and proportionate share of the national economy.
Whatever political theorists may say, or whatever political opportunists may claim, we are still a federal state, not a unitary state and not a state with a very strong centre and very weak parts. In Canada it should never be a question of a central government that is stronger or weaker than the provincial governments, or vice versa. Our constitutional problem should only be to preserve a fair balance between the two types of government. Our constitutional basis provides, and for very good and proven reasons, for certain matters to be handled by a central government and certain others to be administered by regional or provincial governments.
The essential thing is to ensure that each type of government is guaranteed the freedom and the financial muscle to discharge its constitutional responsibilities. I am one of those who is hopeful that the proposed committee will be able to make the existing constitution work without change or, at least, with the minimum of change.
I have mentioned that recent governments have abused our constitution and that Prime ministers, in particular the present one, have assumed extraordinary powers. To me, one of the most obvious and damaging examples of this abuse of the constitution is in the deliberate exclusion by a variety of means of the monarchy from our processes of government. Let me emphasize strongly that when I speak of the monarchy I speak of it only as an institution, a constitutional device that happens also to be the core of our particular system of parliamentary democracy.
I believe it is wrong and would merely be misleading to argue, as many do, for or against the monarchy on grounds of sentimental attachment or emotion. It is not the

January 26. 1970
Canadian Constitution
person of the monarch we must be concerned about, but the institution of the monarchy. The only question to be asked about the monarchy is this: Is it a sound and useful piece of political and constitutional machinery; is it effective in governing a modern state democratically and in freedom; and is it as good as, or better than, other expedients available?
The fact is that our system of government is laid down in our written constitution. The British North America Act, in section 17, under part IV entitled "Legislative Power," says:
There shall be One Parliament for Canada consisting of the Queen, an Upper House styled the Senate, and the House of Commons.
So, whether we like it or not, the sovereign is constitutionally an integral part of our government. To slight or ignore the sovereign, as successive Liberal governments have done in recent years, affects the sovereign but little; it merely demeans and weakens our system of government and the nation. I am convinced that the oblique attacks on the monarchy in this country have less to do with political and constitutional requirements of a modern state than with anti-British sentiments and emotional resentment of pomp and ceremony. If I am correct in that, I think this is an even weaker and more dangerous argument than is sentimental attachment to the royal family.
If you take the trouble to read the story of the birth and early times of confederation, I am sure you will discover, Mr. Speaker, that there were very few colonists in North America of that day who held any sentimental attachment to Great Britain or any love for things or people English. The colonies of those days, the colonies that banded together to form Canada, were settled by many people who had little cause to love England. There were Scottish immigrants driven from their ancestral homes by English influence. There were communities of people who had fled England for religious freedom. There were those of French descent only recently losers in a war against England.
Even the United Empire Loyalists, who had come to the British North American colonies to get away from the new republicanism to the south, had done so more because they preferred British-style government and British institutions than because they loved England. One has only to read of the Loyalists who went to England, instead of what is now Canada, to realize the bitter feeling between the two groups.

Also, we should never forget that one of the chief movers and front-line fighters against the British government in the Lower Canadian rebellion of 1837 was not a French Canadian but a direct descendant of United Empire Loyalists, Dr. Wolfred Nelson.
The facts of the matter are that it was not ties with England and sentimental attachment to that country that prompted our ancestors to opt for the monarchical system of parliamentary democracy. It was shrewd and unemotional assessment that British methods and institutions of democratic government were preferable to the available alternatives.
Recent history has borne out this contention, I believe. In Britain's former colonies, some of which have detached themselves completely from the mother country while others have maintained varying kinds of loose association, British forms of government and British institutions have been retained and cherished. It is significant that India, a country that apparently had little cause to indulge in any sentimental tie with Britain, retained a British form of parliamentary democracy and a judicial and other governmental systems identical to those introduced in the days of British rule.
It is true that India abolished the office of Governor-General and recognizes the sovereign only as the head of the Commonwealth, but she retained the substance of British parliamentary, democratic government. The only real change was to substitute a president as head of state rather than the British reigning monarch. In my view this is no advantage. A president must be chosen. This means the office immediately becomes a political one, no matter how restricted the powers of the president may be. This, to my mind, destroys one of the chief advantages of hereditary monarchy, namely, that it provides a truly non-political figure at the head of government.
I happen to believe we should retain the system of government that incorporates a hereditary and non-political monarch. I do so, however, on grounds of constitutional effectiveness, not because I am misty-eyed about royalty. I also believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is essential today that the question of retaining or abandoning the monarchy be brought out in the open and debated dispassionately on grounds of its worth as an institution and its entrenched position as an essential part of our system of government. I think it is damaging to our social and political stability
January 26, 1970

Canadian Constitution
to stand by and watch a few determined antimonarchists destroy the effectiveness of the institution by ridicule, innuendo and unconstitutional trickery. I think it particularly damaging because I believe this is being done strictly on grounds of anti-British sentiment and for political expediency.
It is my hope that this point will be one of the principal ones discussed by the committee that is proposed. As for curbing the first minister's appetite for dictatorial powers, I believe this, too, must be given priority before Parliament is relegated to the role of a constitutional museum and this country sinks into authoritarian socialism. It would be amusing, if it were not so tragic, to hear people crying for a greater degree of centralized governmental power when this trend runs so directly opposite to the political slogan of this government, "Participatory democracy". The more power is centralized in Ottawa, the further government is removed from the people. This is not peculiar to the federal scene. It occurs at all levels, including provincial and municipal. But it is a fact of modern life that our young people have recognized and against which they are protesting.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
We believe that if democracy is to mean anything, everyone must have the opportunity to be heard and to sway government policy to the best of his or her ability. Canada is a union of regions and cannot be remolded at this stage of development into a unitary state. If the pressure for centralized power persists, it will shatter confederation and fragment its parts beyond reuniting. The Fathers of Confederation knew this well. They recognized this basic fact and wrote the constitution accordingly. All that is needed today is some of their practical common sense and a genuine desire to make our constitution work.
Hear, hear!

Decentralization, not
more centralization, is the only apparent way of adequately protecting regions and minorities in this country and of giving these regions a fair and reasonable voice in their own and national affairs. It is the only manner in which Canadians can be given the chance of close participation in their own affairs.
We have heard a great deal about the concept of the "global village" and that Canada is shrinking in on itself because of great 21611-411
advances in the technology of transportation and communication. The truth is that it is not a homogeneous whole and probably never will be. As for technological advances, if they are so dramatic, how is it that it takes a simple letter ten days to be delivered to Alberta from Ottawa?
Oh, oh!

The hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) has advised me that it took 16 days for a first-class parcel post package with $5 postage to be delivered from Toronto to Moncton.
My idea of Canada is a national government politically, constitutionally and financially, strong enough to discharge its constitutional responsibilities and, when necessary, to assist in keeping the various regions in economic balance-and no more. With this concept I see regional governments equally strongly situated to discharge their regional responsibilities. I say regional rather than provincial because it may well be that amalgamation of one or more provinces will eventually make better economic sense in this country.
If total government spending were limited to a percentage of the gross national product, all governments would then have to work for policies which would increase the size of the pie for all if they were desirous of increasing their spending, instead of the present situation where all they do is increase their slice of the pie at the expense of the citizen. To achieve this balance of power and strength between governments, I believe it has now become necessary to bolster it with constitutional provisions that would effectively prevent encroachment of the federal government on the regional governments.
One of the great areas of federal excess has been not only its own profligate spending but the pressure exerted on provinces to spend. This has been apparent in many so-called "national" programs, such as medicare where a combination of federal manipulation and political blackmail forced many provinces to commit themselves over their financial head.
