I believe that one of our great troubles today is that those who enjoy power do not understand our constitutional heritage. They in fact appear to despise it and would change it, without any reference to the Canadian people, by subtle and unconstitutional means. Having no regard for the constitution, it has been easy for them to find ways around it.

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
This fact alone has caused me to change my mind to a certain extent and to now believe that some constitutional safeguards for the constitution itself should be incorporated. We must aim at making it impossible for anyone to bypass the constitution and Parliament. If we do not, Canadians will find themselves in the classic position that bred the United States revolution and the twin "taxation without representation". Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may yet enter the history books as the twentieth century's George III, a slimmer Gallic version of Lord North.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I welcome the establishment of a parliamentary committee as a means of adding another dimension to the discussion surrounding our constitution, because in the discussions so far it is apparent to me that some of the provinces for one reason or another are not standing up for their rights as they should be.
I hope the committee will be useful in persuading the government that what is needed in this country is decentralization, that the provinces should be allowed to discharge their responsibilities in respect of education, health services including the ever-expanding problem of mental health and urban transit, and that it is no longer acceptable for the federal government to treat them like beggars.
What I have suggested, Mr. Speaker, really amounts to ways and means of ensuring adherence to our present constitution and to the necessary minimum required to keep Canada together by giving our people a continued feeling of confidence in our nation, a feeling which I think we all believe is beginning to be questioned in many areas of the land.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to contribute to this debate tonight, I do so as a non-expert. I make no apologies for not being a lawyer. I speak as a former businessman and I think I speak for concerned citizens through the land.
I feel the big debate in the next ten years will be on how we at the centre of power will use power or find the power to deal with such questions as pollution, foreign ownership and regulating our economy. Today's citizen is very much aware of the fact that the world as he knows it may not exist in 50 years time because of man's capacity to destroy it through his industrialization. He is aware of the fact that the automobile, through the discharge of exhaust fumes, may in the next 20

years raise the carbon dioxide content of the air to such a level that the temperature of the earth will rise by ten degrees and in so doing the ocean levels will rise six feet or more. Once this happens, it becomes an irreversible process. I suggest to hon. members this is something of considerable and enduring concern to the citizens of Canada.
The Canadian citizen is concerned about foreign ownership and the fact that if we do not find some way to deal with this question we may have no country and no identity by the end of the century. He is concerned about what he thinks are King Canute methods of dealing with the question of inflation. He does not understand that the call for voluntary restraint is no more than a call to those who are most sensitive, to those who are most responsible and an opportunity for those who are less responsible.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
He is not convinced that by asking people to show restraint the tide of inflation will somehow abate. He is concerned that the federal government does not have the power, or so it seems to him. Why else would we be speaking purely in terms of voluntary restraints? Why, for example, does not the federal government have the power to deal with consumer credit? Why does it not have the power to deal with wage, price and dividend restraint? Why does the approach have to be by way of voluntary restraint?
As a member of this House I am impressed, as I know others are impressed, by the initiatives shown by the federal government with respect to the need for constitutional change. Since this government took office there has been a substantial dialogue. As the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. All-mand) mentioned this evening, seven papers have been published dealing with constitutional matters. The last conference, held not very long ago, was attended by certain municipal representatives. This is the first time for a long time that a municipal representative has been included as a member of a delegation; on other occasions municipal representatives have been included as observers. I, for one, hope that future constitutional conferences will see municipal representatives included as members of provincial delegations. In this way, it seems to me, the cities can be included in the dialogue between the provincial governments and the federal government concerning this important area of constitutional change.
January 26. 1970

Canadian Constitution
Citizens, as we all know, will come to us and say, "I really do not understand the problem. .Governments are to serve the interests of the people, and you people argue that you do not have the power; the provincial governments have the power. I go to my provincial member, and he says, 'This is not a question for me; it is a question for your federal member.' " We have all run into this kind of difficulty. We have all been told we are overgoverned and overtaxed. I think the citizen today has begun to wonder increasingly about the nature of the distribution of powers. He is asking the question more and more, "Does the federal government lack the power?" If it lacks the power, let it say so as representative of all Canadians; and let us remind ourselves that we are the only institution in Canada which is representative of all Canadians.
As I say, I do not bring to this debate the knowledge of a constitutional lawyer or of an expert, but there are certain areas to which I should like to draw attention. It seems to me that one of the first principles when solving any problem is to find out whose responsibility it is and then to ensure that there is commensurable authority to go with it. At least, this is the way business deals with problems.
It seems to me that what we lack today is power at the centre. A few moments ago, the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) said what we needed in our constitutional arrangements was greater decentralization. I believe the application of power should be decentralized, but I do not think this is inconsistent with there being greater power at the centre, particularly when dealing with economic matters. As the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) said a short while ago, this is an area wherein we lack substantial power.
Looking at the motion which has been presented to us, I am happy to see that the committee is to be given the power to call witnesses. I am concerned, however, that it does not appear to have the power to hire staff. I hope this is nothing more than an oversight and that the committee will be given power to hire staff. In this connection, I hope, too, that more assistance will be forthcoming to the caucuses. I speak as a member of the Liberal caucus who would much appreciate the kind of assistance which is available to many hon. members opposite in terms of research staff. If the committee system is to work effectively, we must supply committees with the necessary staff.
I hope this special committee will call for a projection of the spending intentions of the provincial governments and the federal government collectively over the next five years and then ask, of qualified witnesses, just what revenue would be forthcoming to the provinces and to the federal government if there were no changes in existing levels of taxation at either the federal or provincial levels.
Let us get this information and place it before the public and members of the House of Commons. Unless we possess information of this kind, the whole question of spending and taxation powers becomes, in part, an academic exercise. If we are to consider the distribution of powers, we must have this information.
The committee should ask the question: Does the federal government possess the authority it needs today to deal with the various threats to our survival? For example, does it have authority to deal with pollution?
Yes.
It has made a start in the Canada water bill. But what about air pollution? Has it all the authority it needs to deal with pollution from automobiles?
Yes.

Has it the necessary authority to deal with industrial pollution? Let us make absolutely clear to all citizens of Canada where the responsibility lies.
Let us consider the field of foreign ownership. The British North America Act, if it was designed to protect the land mass against United States annexation, has been eminently successful. But if it was intended to protect the ownership of our natural resources, it has been a failure. The provincial governments, and particularly the provincial premiers, could not care less, it seems to me, about who owns our natural resources. I suggest that the federal government does not appear to possess the authority to regulate this essential aspect of our national affairs.
Third, with respect to regulating the economy, surely it is time we transferred power to the federal government to regulate consumer credit. Surely it is time we transferred standby powers with respect to the regulation of capital spending. Surely it is time we transferred the necessary power to deal with wages, prices and dividends in times of inflation. If we duck the opportunity presented by the conference coming up in two weeks time,

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
we shall have done a great disservice to ourselves and to this nation. I trust the committee will direct itself to these questions.

Mr. Speaker, to my mind the Canadian Parliament is debating an extremely important matter. The official opposition has repeatedly requested, since 1965, the appointment of a parliamentary committee on the Canadian constitution. We did not do so to embarrass the government in power but because we were convinced that this was both urgent and necessary.
Four stands have been adopted to date in the face of the Canadian constitutional crisis.
The first, that of the status quo, does not meet the objectives of the provinces; this was quite obvious at the last constitutional conference at which time the provinces demanded immediate amendments. As we know, the powers are not well divided. There is duplication in the activities, and the present constitution does not meet the needs of our modern times.
The second, which is as extreme as the first and, obviously, just as unacceptable, advocates total decentralization of powers in favour of the provinces. This attitude was advocated especially by certain Quebec groups and would require the creation of associate states. Let us face the facts: this tenent is unacceptable because it would mean the end of Canada. In fact there would be two states, or more if other provinces took advantage of the right to decentralization.
The third, we also reject: it is that of the present government. It consists in the centralization of powers, and denies the provinces the possibility of playing a dynamic role within the Canadian confederation.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Finally there is the fourth, which I shall describe in a moment. It seems logical to us, members from Quebec, because it does not treat the provinces as agencies of the central government, but as useful, active and responsible members within the Canadian confederation. That principle has been advocated repeatedly, as well in Quebec as elsewhere. It strikes us as much more acceptable.
That is the way Quebecers now see the constitutional crisis, and how the majority of them feel it can be overcome.
It must be admitted from the start that Quebec is not just another province. This has

been proclaimed for the past hundred years. Five-sixths of Canada's French-speaking population live in Quebec and that is what makes it different from the other provinces.
Other differences could also be mentioned, resulting from Quebec's geographic position, commanding the main route of communication toward the interior of the continent. It could also be said that Quebec is different because of its immense untapped reserves of natural resources. Merely taking into account that it is different because its population is primarily and predominantly French-speaking, it must be recognized that Quebec can enrich Canada, if it is to be different from its southern neighbour.
On many occasions, French-Canadiens have expressed dissatisfaction about their status within the Canadian confederation. In fact, one only has to read the report of the Tremblay Commission, the report of the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, and the statements from all the Quebec premiers, Liberal or Union Nationale, at the constitutional conferences, and more especially since 1960, to become aware of the continuity in Quebec's demands.
This government has always claimed to be sympathetic to Quebec's requests, but so far, it has done nothing about them. It may say that it has passed an official languages bill, with our consent. Yet, everyone knows very well that both languages have been recognized and protected in Quebec for a long time, and that the government passed that bill, after several years of delay and hesitation, much more to favour French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec.
The government has therefore done nothing to allow Quebec to follow its cultural vocation. Quebecers are more and more conscious of the role they can play in Canadian life, or of the lack of it. Unless they are allowed to take an active part, it is to be feared that they might decide to leave Confederation.
Separatism is a dreadful threat. And that is something Quebec members have to live with every day. Even though we know that separatism could have harmful effects on both Canada and Quebec, it still remains a possibility.
To realize it, it is enough to consider how Quebecers are getting more and more indifferent to federal politics. At the last election, the percentage of the Quebec vote was the lowest in the country; 72 per cent, compared to 78 per cent in 1963.
January 26, 1970

The government should not either bow to Quebecers' claims just to cajole them, to keep them of its side; that would be hypocritical.
The requests of Quebec must therefore be given the importance they deserve, because we are convinced that Quebec has its place within the Canadian confederation and that its particular charasteristics can play a precious role. It is by acknowledging these characteristics of Quebec that Canadian unity will be achieved, on the basis of equality of the two founding nations, whatever word may be used to designate the two ethnic entities which exist in Canada. The main thing is to realize that Canada has two majority groups which are sociologically different. Contrary to what the Prime Minister said during the election campaign, it does not mean that there are two countries within a single state, because that is not what the people of Quebec want. Since they want to live in a single country, the majority of Canadians must also recognize the differences which may benefit confederation.
It is not enough to recognize that the province of Quebec is different; it must be recognized also that it is in a position to discharge a very large part of the responsibilities issuing from that difference. In the area of culture, we see that these last few years, the province of Quebec has increased its connections and its relations with the French-speaking world. Because its main group is of French culture, the province of Quebec must allow that group to live more intensely in French, and to add to its culture.
How can we expect five million Frenchspeaking people, on a continent inhabited by 220 million English-speaking people, to be self-sufficient insofar as culture is concerned? To the extent that the human body needs fresh air, the French-speaking civilization needs sources on which to feed.
But whenever Quebec tried to improve its relations and enter into agreements with French-speaking countries, the federal government showed its displeasure and opposed any such move. Don't we French Canadians from Quebec have every reason to wonder why in the course of the last 60 or 70 years the federal government did not choose to strengthen its contacts with French-speaking countries in order to meet the cultural requirements of the Quebec people as well as those of other French-speaking Canadians?
There is no doubt that Quebec has greatly benefited and still benefits by these agreements with French-speaking nations. Let us
Canadian Constitution
mention for instance the numerous exchanges of teachers, students, technicians and experts as well as the increase of French investments in Quebec.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
If Quebec benefits from such exchanges and agreements, the rest of Canada is in no way deprived. By increasing such exchanges with the French-speaking world, Quebec does not deprive anyone of anything. We should, rather, rejoice that Quebec benefits so greatly from them.
Besides, no objections were ever raised against Ontario having offices in different countries, in England for instance, because this could promote its culture and its interests. The federal government did not raise any objections either when Ontario instituted in its Department of Education a Cultural Exchanges Division and signed agreements, with France amongst others, for exchanges of students and professors.
However, Mr. Speaker, if Quebec dares take some steps in this direction, the central government first objects, to agree later on, as was the case for the conferences of the Education Ministers of French-speaking countries; on the other hand, if it does not agree to it, it intimidates the countries which would like to have relations with Quebec as was the case when diplomatic relations with Gabon were broken up.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, these are unpleasant facts to hear but the truth has to be spoken before our English-speaking Canadian friends, here in this sanctuary which is the House of Commons.
It is not just in the field of culture that Quebec needs to take steps in order to fulfill this characteristic. There is the field of social welfare, the field of immigration, the field of education which belongs to Quebec and to the provinces, but where the federal government continues to withhold the amounts Quebec would need for its administration, under the pretense that in its opinion, these amounts must be used for university education.
However, university education does not come under federal jurisdiction, at least in our opinion. The Quebec government is quite able to look after its education system properly and to decide what amounts of money must be allocated without any conditions being set by the central government especially in matters such as education or health which, under the constitution, come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.

January 26, 1970
Canadian Constitution
Therefore, why deny Quebec the right to have specific needs, when the premiers of Ontario and Manitoba have stated, following the last constitutional conference, that they had no objection to Quebec having special arrangements within the Canadian Confederation, in order to meet all the needs of that majority of French Canadians who live now in this beautiful country that we call Canada?
Mr. Speaker, that is the question that we must put to the government. Why this obstinate refusal of the fact that Quebec is not a province like the others? It is only a question of thinking of a new constitution in which jurisdictions will be negotiated and Quebec could be a part of a federation by playing in it a dynamic role and by meeting its own particular requirements. The federal government must not only allow Quebec to play a role in meeting its particular needs, but they should also, if they want to keep Quebec within Confederation, do all they can to enable Quebec to achieve its aims.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a concession that must be granted to Quebec and Quebecers are not asking the central government for gifts when they speak in this way. I say that Quebec has a right to demand these realities which enable Canada to be a great country because it is a bicultural and bilingual one.
Mr. Speaker, we have reached a point where a clear and precise decision must be made. We must no longer expect that time will settle things well because it will not do that from now on, in Quebec. Indeed, Quebec has been patient. It put forth its point of view on many occasions. It will keep on doing it for some time but there are limits to its patience-I repeat, there are limits to its patience.
It should be made quite clear that when Quebec is asking for special arrangements, it does not mean to deprive anybody in any way. We hope the federal government will show good will and understanding. In order to help it arrive at a fair decision, the members of the Progressive Conservative party again suggest to establish a parliamentary committee on the constitution which, in my view, should enjoy very extensive terms of reference, enabling it to consider the reform of both the Senate and of the Supreme Court.
It should also be entrusted with the task of considering the establishment of a constitutional court where the differences between the provinces and the central government could be better settled than by the Supreme

Court of Canada whose decisions, in the past, have often been challenged by the provinces.
Moreover, a parliamentary committee on the constitution should study the whole question of the monarchy and that of the establishment of a presidential system. Those are questions asked by the young people nowadays. I am not saying this in order to promote one system more than the other, but to bring forward the ideals of the young Canadians who call for a constitution, not only for the present but for the future of those who wish to keep on militating in the Canadian Confederation.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are getting ready to tell me that my time has expired but I will take only a few more minutes.
Since 1965 we have called for the establishment of this committee but in vain. We are happy today that the government put that question before the House. We are ready to do our share so that a sound dialogue may begin between all parts of the Canadian federation, so that a new constitution may soon be drafted, which will meet all the needs and ideals of all the Canadian people.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, in 1964 Members of Parliament from the New Democratic Party proposed the establishment of a House of Commons committee to discuss and study the problems involved in amending or changing the constitution. At that time the proposal was rejected by the government and has consistently until today been rejected.
We endorse the idea of a committee to study the constitution and needed changes to it, because we recognize the tremendous difficulties which have occurred in this country since the constitution was written and adopted more than 100 years ago. One hundred years ago when the British North America Act was enacted, this country was essentially rural. Today, a substantial majority of the people of Canada live in the cities.
When the constitution was adopted, the federal government allocated to itself those powers and responsibilities which it considered important and left to the provinces those responsibilities which at that time it considered to be much less essential and important to the people. The judgement of the federal government at that time probably was correct, but the urbanization of this country has
January 26, 1970

made a tremendous difference. Therefore, we now find that some of the most important functions in respect of the day-to-day life of the people of this country have been left, under the provisions of the constitution, to the provinces.
The provinces, in turn, over the years have given a great deal of that responsibility to the cities which are entirely creatures of the provincial governments. This government and its Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have until now taken the position that our constitution is essentially a good constitution; that if we are in trouble it is because the federal government has not stuck to its jurisdiction and the responsibilities given it under the constitution and that the provinces, similarly, have not stuck to their responsibilities under the constitution.
The major field in which the Prime Minister feels the federal government must have responsibility, and the one thing which he has wanted to discuss with the provinces in respect of changes in the constitution, concerns the French-speaking people of Canada. The Prime Minister feels that regardless of where they live, they must be given equal rights with English-speaking Canadians in the use of their language in all parts of Canada.
We in our party have agreed with that part of the proposition put forward by the Prime Minister. We have done so even though many of our constituents have not understood what the Prime Minister was talking about and what we were trying to do. We have agreed with this because we feel it essential that if this country is to survive as one country, the French-speaking people must be given the feeling they are equal citizens. However, the people in English-speaking Canada and in French-speaking Canada need more than the right to use the English or French language in any part of Canada; they must start dealing with the many problems of modern-day life with which they have not had an opportunity to deal.
If there is criticism of the approach of this government and the Prime Minister in many parts of Canada-and there is-it is not based on partisan, political reasons. I should like to point out to members of this House what I am sure they already know. There is no harsher critic of the government and the Prime Minister in respect of the approach taken to the constitution than the Liberal Premier of the province of Saskatchewan. If I were to use some of the language he has used, I am cer-

We all know that the former minister of transport and deputy prime minister resigned from the cabinet because of his feeling that if we accepted the views of the Prime Minister about the constitution in respect of problems such as housing, it would be impossible to deal with the problems of the cities and find a solution to them.
I could spend more than the time I have in putting on the record the point of view of the Liberal member for York West (Mr. Givens), a former mayor of Toronto, who outside this chamber has spoken repeatedly about the failure of this government and its Prime Minister to face up to the responsibilities which a federal government must assume if it is to meet the problems of the cities. It is because of my feeling that this government is taking too narrow and too legalistic a position in respect of amending and changing the constitution that I rise today to speak in this debate.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, prior to the Christmas recess I asked a question of the Postmaster General (Mr. Kier-ans), the Minister of Communications or whatever the father of our new jet-age postal system now styles himself. It went without answer, and that it is the reason I am discussing it at this time, because it touches on the sad state to which a fundamental public service has degenerated. The question had to do with the announcement that the minister had appointed a senior productivity executive to his staff. As I understood the minister's announcement of this appointment, the prime duty of this extra official would be to combat inflation in the workings of the Post Office Department.
This struck me as a classic example of putting the cart before the horse. The minister had set the process of unrestrained inflation in motion long before hiring someone to con-
January 26, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion trol it. I am talking about the minister's great reform, the imposition of primitive and crippling new postal rates on the Canadian public. His stated reason was to enable the Post Office Department to operate like a healthy private business concern at a profit. He has not yet explained from whence he received his mandate to turn a vital public service into a private money-making proposition.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

maintopic: POST OFFICE-ASSIGNMENT OF NEW PRODUCTIVITY EXECUTIVE
speechtext:
What we need in his department is an official to bring back our fast and reliable postal service and to reduce excessively high postal rates, not a man to draw a very large salary for tilting at windmills.
Ever since 1840 when Sir Rowland Hill introduced the first cheap and effective public postal service in Great Britain, the Post Office and its work has been recognized as a basic public service for which the taxpayer was willing to pay something in support out of the public funds. It had two aims-to carry the mail as cheaply as possible and to be as reliable as possible. These have since been the aims of almost every civilized country in the operation of their postal services.
But this was P.K. I do not mean pre-Cambrian, but pre-Kierans. Now we have a new apostle and a new creed: To the devil with what people want and in support of which they are willing to pay taxes. We know better. We will make this service pay even if it means fewer mail deliveries, long delays, and much higher rates.
The minister worshipped too long at the shrine of private industry as president of the Montreal Stock Exchange, without learning anything. He is infatuated by profit for the sake of profit.
The questions I pose this evening are simply these: When will the Postmaster General stop destroying the identity of countless small localities by closing down post offices? When will he and his army of efficiency experts restore the reliability of our mail delivery system? When will he come to his senses and lower postal rates to make the postal service once more a public service and not a luxury? When will he stop trying to "snow" the public with science-fiction press releases, and get his department back on the track?

maintopic: MANPOWER-ADULT RETRAINING AND EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMS-ALLEGED WASTING OF MONEY
MANPOWER-ADULT RETRAINING AND EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMS-ALLEGED WASTING OF MONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 5 I brought to the attention of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) the charges made in a report prepared for the Association of Colleges of Arts and Technology of Ontario that the manpower training program operated by the federal government was inefficient, wasteful, and was not doing the job of training people who are out of work, which it was set up to do. Manpower training began in 1961 under the former Conservative government as a joint program financed and administered both by the federal government and the provincial governments. In 1967 the manpower training program was taken out of the hands of the provincial governments. Schools coming under the jurisdiction of the provinces are used for the training of manpower, but the entire responsibility for the program now rests with the federal government.
Because the federal government has the sole responsibility, and because there has been a lamentable lack of co-operation with the provincial governments and the local schools in which the manpower training programs are conducted, the colleges to which I have referred made a report which deserves to be discussed and will be discussed in detail when the estimates of the department come before the appropriate parliamentary committee.
The report says that the manpower training programs have become not really training programs but primarily programs designed to put people to work as quickly as possible whether they have the training required for

January 26, 1970

permanent work and whether the available jobs are suitable or not. The main responsibility undertaken by the department seems to be to put a person into a job, a slot, if that can be accomplished. It is only after the person repeatedly fails on a job that the department considers an adequate program of manpower training. The report charges that the bureaucracy and red-tape have multiplied to such an extent that the people who need the training, simply become discouraged and give up.
What are some of the problems? One is the decision that no manpower training program may last more than a year, 52 weeks. But a large percentage of our population, the Metis people in particular but also people from many of the rural areas of Eastern and Western Canada, have only grade six or grade seven education. They cannot fit into existing training programs and apprenticeship programs. The one year for which they are paid a training allowance sometimes brings them only to the grade eight, nine or 10 level of education. What they need is the equivalent of grade 12. But for those unfortunate enough to live in areas that do not provide facilities-and this is all too true of many areas in this country, and probably in no province is it as prevalent as the minister's province of Nova Scotia-all the 52 weeks' training does is bring them to grade eight level. It simply does not give them the background necessary to take the technical training that they require.
The other thing, Mr. Speaker, is that the Manpower Department has built up its own organization and there is little co-operation between the department and the school facilities. There are counsellors working for the Manpower Department and counsellors working for the education authorities, but according to the report to which I have referred, the co-operation between them leaves a great deal to be desired. Those who suffer are the people taking the training.
One other aspect to which I have referred again and again in debates about manpower training is this: The counsellors employed by the Manpower Department have virtually life and death power in respect of the program. They decide whether a person shall take a job or shall take further education; they decide whether a person shall take the training in his own city or in another, and they decide how long he shall be entitled to the training. According to the report, the co-operation between the manpower counsellors and 21611-42*

Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons I would urge the minister to study the report made by educational people who have had long experience in working with those needing education and who are in day-to-day contact with this problem. I ask that the difficulties referred to in this report, which are dealt with in much more detail than I could hope to do, be studied objectively and without partisanship.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has referred to a report that was issued some time ago and he bases his statements on the contents of that report. At the time the report was issued, and before a copy had been delivered to me, there was extensive reporting in the newspapers. At that time I made a public comment indicating that in my view the report did not represent a very fair or balanced picture of the operation of the Canada Manpower training program. The report itself is under review in my department, and the findings up to the present time give us no reason for changing the original analysis or reaction to it.
My hon. friend has mentioned a relatively large number of issues which I cannot deal with in a couple of minutes. We co-operate with the provinces. The successful operation of our program depends on close co-operation and collaboration with all provincial governments. Last week my deputy had meetings with all the deputy ministers of the provinces to consider how the program could be improved and how the process of consultation could be enhanced. Also, the hon. member should know that recently we had a meeting with ministers from the province of Manitoba, and part of the agenda dealt with ways and means of increasing co-operation in order to make the program more effective.
I had a meeting with the Minister of Education of Manitoba and we reached a good understanding as to how the program might be applied in that province to meet the particular needs of various communities. So, to suggest that there is minimal co-operation is inaccurate. We could not contemplate spending so much money in training the large numbers of people involved without having the close co-operation of the provinces.
We have conducted extensive cost-benefit analyses of the results of this program. We

maintopic: POLLUTION-DUMPING OF OIL AND OTHER WASTE IN GREAT LAKES
POLLUTION-DUMPING OF OIL AND OTHER WASTE IN GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 5, almost two months ago, I directed the following question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene):
Having regard to the fact that the United States government recommended two days ago to the Canada-United States International Joint Commission that a moratorium with respect to oil drilling in Lake Erie be imposed because of the dangerous pollution possibilities, would the minister indicate whether the Canadian government intends to make a similar representation to the International Joint Commission?
I welcome this opportunity to give a little more background to my question and trust that we will hear from the minister tonight whether the Canadian government has also recommended to the Canada-United States International Joint Commission that a similar moratorium with respect to oil-drilling in Lake Erie be imposed.
It seems to me that in the mad search for resources the various levels of government often failed to take into account any adverse effects which the development and use of the resource might have on our total environment. In many instances permits for exploration and development are granted without proper safeguards being insisted upon by the governments involved. Frequently we find that governments have completely overlooked the possibility of major ecological damage being done and certainly have not weighed these chances, however remote they may be, against the over-all return from any given resource. A good example of this lack of foresight is found in the oil-drilling permits which have been allowed in Lake Erie.

In a news story in the Toronto Telegram of December 4,	1969, the following report
appeared:
The United States government recommended to the United States-Canada International Joint Commission yesterday a moratorium on oil well drilling in heavily polluted Lake Erie.
Kenneth Bigland, Director of the United States Federal Water Pollution Control Administration's Division of Technological Support, said both planning and methods of dealing with oil spills on the lake remained limited. He said the moratorium should extend to natural gas drilling where such wells are likely to produce crude oil above specified levels, but he said the moratorium would not necessarily affect gas production which is already under way on the Canadian side of the lake.
Other interesting points have been raised in connection with oil-drilling in Lake Erie. It has been pointed out that one of the greatest dangers posed by drilling would be an accidental leak of the salt brine used. Apparently experts have warned that a spill of salt brine from an oil well would be one of the greatest natural catastrophes that could strike the Great Lakes. However, this is one aspect of pollution about which we have heard very little.
The main point I would like to make this evening, is that the recent IJC hearings clearly demonstrated that we do not have the facilities in the Great Lakes area to deal with a possible major oil well leak, or a major spill of oil from a sinking tanker. It would be utter catastrophe if a major spill of oil took place in any one of the Great Lakes. The hearing has pinpointed the fact that there is conflict between the federal and provincial jurisdictions as far as responsibility is concerned.
It appears that we have no contingency plans to deal with possible major oil well leaks such as the one off the coast of California last January. It appears that the lack of proper co-ordination between the federal and the provincial authorities is very much in evidence. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this problem should be tackled without delay. I feel the federal government should also recommend that drilling for gas and oil in Lake Erie be suspended until we can practically guarantee that these recreational areas will not be permanently destroyed by a major oil spill.
We have huge reserves of oil all over this nation, and there is no need to jeopardize Lake Erie or any of the Great Lakes which go to make up the greatest body of fresh water to be found anywhere in the world. This is a precious heritage to be protected. We cannot afford to take a chance on it with the appar-
January 26, 1970	COMMONS
ent inadequate facilities and safeguards now available to us. I urge the minister and the government to re-examine this problem and, in this instance to go along with the United States government in recommending the discontinuance of drilling until adequate safeguards are available.
